{{Short description|American actress (born 1957)}} {{use mdy dates|date=July 2019}} {{Infobox person | name = Nana Visitor | image = Nana Visitor GalaxyCon Oklahoma City 052026-4.jpg | caption = Visitor at [[GalaxyCon]] Oklahoma City in 2026 | birth_name = Nana Tucker | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1957|7|26}} | birth_place = New York City, U.S. | occupation = Actress | years_active = 1976–present | spouse = {{plainlist| * {{marriage|Nick Miscusi|1989|1994|end=divorced}} * {{marriage|[[Alexander Siddig]]|1997|2001|end=divorced}} * {{marriage|Matthew Rimmer
|2003}} }} | children = 2 | relatives = [[Paris Theodore]] (half-brother)
[[Cyd Charisse]] (aunt) }} '''Nana Visitor''' ({{IPAc-en|n|ə|ˈ|n|ɑː}} {{respell|nə|NAH}};{{cite web|title=Star Trek Infinite Space: Nana Visitor & Rene Auberjonois Interview|via = YouTube|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cBNHwmz_pHA|access-date=November 12, 2023|date=September 28, 2011}} born '''Nana Tucker'''; July 26, 1957) is an American actress, best known for playing Major, later Colonel, [[Kira Nerys]] in the television series ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' and Jean Ritter in the television series ''[[Wildfire (2005 TV series)|Wildfire]]''. ==Early life== Nana Tucker was born July 26, 1957, in New York City,{{cite web |url = http://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/nana-visitor/190655 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080203065144/http://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/nana-visitor/190655 |url-status = dead |archive-date = February 3, 2008 |title = Nana Visitor |work = [[TV Guide]] |access-date = September 7, 2011 }} the daughter of Nenette Charisse, a ballet teacher, and Robert Tucker, a choreographer; she is a niece of actress/dancer [[Cyd Charisse]].{{cite web |url = http://www.filmreference.com/film/4/Nana-Visitor.html |title = Nana Visitor Biography (1957–) |work = Film Reference. |access-date = August 12, 2013 }} ==Career== {{refimprove|section|date=October 2026}} Visitor began her acting career in the 1970s on the [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] stage in such productions as ''[[My One and Only (musical)|My One and Only]]''.{{cite web|title=Nana Visitor|url=http://www.playbill.com/person/nana-visitor-vault-0000044934|work = Playbill |access-date=28 July 2018}} Her film debut (billed by her birth name, Nana Tucker) came in the 1977 horror film ''[[The Sentinel (1977 film)|The Sentinel]].'' On television, Visitor co-starred in the short-lived 1976 sitcom ''[[Ivan the Terrible (TV series)|Ivan the Terrible]]'' and from 1978 to 1982, had short-lived regular roles on three soap operas: ''[[Ryan's Hope]],'' ''[[The Doctors (soap opera)|The Doctors]],'' and ''[[One Life to Live]].'' Upon the suggestion of her older brother Paris, she adopted the stage name "Nana Visitor" in the early 1980s,{{cite web |url=https://vm.tiktok.com/ZMFop1s3m/ |format=TikTok |title=Star Trek Nana Visitor Talks about her stage name |accessdate=2023-01-13 }} and had her name legally changed to "Visitor" some time later.{{cite podcast| url= https://scpod.net/episodes/star-trek-deep-space-nines-nana-visitor-commander-kira-nerys| title= Star Trek Deep Space Nine's Nana Visitor| website=Spoiler Country| last1=Regan|first1=Kenric|last2=Horsley|first2=John| date=28 July 2020| time=00:20:00| access-date=13 November 2024}}{{cite podcast| url= https://patreon.com/posts/113868024| title= The Delta Flyers - DS9 Crossover 223| website=The Delta Flyers| last1=McNeill|first1=Robert Duncan|last2=Wang|first2=Garrett|last3=Shimerman|first3=Armin| date=14 October 2024| time=02:34:00| access-date=13 November 2024}} In 1984, she appeared in a season-two episode of ''[[Hunter (1984 U.S. TV series)|Hunter]].'' In 1985, Visitor made appearances on the television series ''[[MacGyver (1985 TV series)|MacGyver]],'' in the season-one episode "Hellfire" as Laura Farren, and in the season-two episode "DOA: MacGyver" as Carol Varnay. She also made an appearance in the fourth-season ''[[Remington Steele]]'' episode titled "Steele Blushing" the same year. In 1986, she appeared in "Hills of Fire", a fourth-season episode of ''[[Knight Rider (1982 TV series)|Knight Rider]],'' as well as third-season ''[[Highway to Heaven]]'' episodes "Love at Second Sight" and "Love and Marriage, Part II" as Margaret Swann. In 1987, Visitor appeared as Ellen Dolan in a failed [[television pilot]] for Will Eisner's pulp comic creation ''[[The Spirit (character)|The Spirit]],'' starring [[Sam J. Jones]] as the title character and [[Garry Walberg]] as her father, Commissioner Dolan. [[File:Nana Visitor STICCon 2004 crop.jpg|thumb|right|upright|Visitor at STICCon XVIII (2004)]] In 1988, she made an appearance on the sitcom ''[[Night Court]]'' as a mental patient who is obsessed with the movies. That same year, she made an appearance on the television series ''[[In the Heat of the Night (TV series)|In the Heat of the Night]]'' as the owner of the Sparta newspaper. She also made an appearance that year in an episode of ''[[Matlock (1986 TV series)|Matlock]].'' In 1989, Visitor appeared in the fifth episode of the television series ''[[Doogie Howser, M.D.]]'' as Charmagne, a rock star who has a throat nodule removed at Doogie's hospital, and as Miles Drentell's glamorous girlfriend, in "Success", a 1989 episode of ''[[Thirtysomething (TV series)|Thirtysomething]]''{{'}}s second season. In 1990, Visitor co-starred with [[Sandra Bullock]] in the short-lived sitcom ''[[Working Girl (TV series)|Working Girl]],'' which was based on the feature film of the same name. From 1993 to 1999, Visitor appeared in ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' as Major (later Colonel) [[Kira Nerys]], a former freedom fighter/terrorist from the planet Bajor, who fought against the occupation of her world by the [[Cardassians]]. After the occupation ended, she was appointed as first officer of the series's eponymous space station, built by the Cardassians and turned over to [[Starfleet]]. She revisited the character, as a voice actress, in the third season of the animated series ''[[Star Trek: Lower Decks]]''.{{cite web |last1=Orquiola |first1=John |title="It Made No Sense": DS9 Actor Explains Her Plan To Also Play Star Trek: Voyager's Captain Janeway |date=June 18, 2025 |url=https://screenrant.com/star-trek-ds9-nana-visitor-voyager-janeway-both-roles/ |publisher=Screen Rant |access-date=21 June 2025}} She was also interested to play the character of [[Kathryn Janeway]] in the series ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'', filmed at the same time.{{cite web |last1=Pascale |first1=Anthony |title=Interview: Nana Visitor On Wanting To Play Janeway On 'Voyager' And The Future Of Kira Nerys In 'Star Trek' |url=https://trekmovie.com/2025/06/17/interview-nana-visitor-on-wanting-to-play-janeway-on-voyager-and-the-future-of-kira-nerys-in-star-trek/ |publisher=Trekmovie |access-date=21 June 2025}} [[File:Visitor and Auberjonois by Beth Madison, 2.jpg|thumb|left|Nana Visitor and [[Rene Auberjonois]] at the 2011 Star Trek convention in Las Vegas]] After ''DS9'' ended, Visitor had a recurring role as villain Dr. Elizabeth Renfro on the television series ''[[Dark Angel (2000 TV series)|Dark Angel]].'' Visitor then starred as Roxie Hart in both the touring and Broadway companies of the musical ''[[Chicago (musical)|Chicago]],''{{cite web|url=http://www.playbill.com/article/nana-visitor-is-foxy-roxie-hart-in-bways-chicago-beginning-may-8-com-96505|title=Nana Visitor Is Foxy Roxie Hart in Bway's ''Chicago'' Beginning May 8|last=Jones|first=Kenneth|date=8 May 2001|website=[[Playbill]]|access-date=28 July 2018}} including starring as Hart as curtains rose again after September 11, 2001. Visitor was then cast as Jean Ritter on the [[Freeform (TV channel)|ABC Family]] series ''[[Wildfire (2005 TV series)|Wildfire]],'' which premiered on June 20, 2005. In 2008, she appeared as Emily Kowalski, a dying cancer patient in "[[Faith (Battlestar Galactica)|Faith]]", an episode of the reimagined ''[[Battlestar Galactica (2004 TV series)|Battlestar Galactica]]''{{'}}s fourth season. Visitor had a small role as [[Pamela Voorhees]] in the 2009 version of ''[[Friday the 13th (2009 film)|Friday the 13th]].'' She has also lent her voice in a few appearances on the sitcom ''[[Family Guy]],'' such as Rita in the episode "[[Brian's Got a Brand New Bag]]", and as the voice of the [[USS Enterprise (NCC-1701)|''Enterprise'']] in "[[Extra Large Medium]]." In 2011, she had a small part in the Hammer Horror film ''[[The Resident (film)|The Resident]],'' playing the realtor. She appeared in ''[[Torchwood: Miracle Day]]'' episodes seven ("[[Immortal Sins]]") and eight ("[[End of the Road (Torchwood)|End of the Road]]").{{cite journal |title=Horror Flicks |date=June 2011| journal=[[Doctor Who Magazine]]| issue=435}} In 2012, she appeared as Dr. Patty Barker, a canine psychotherapist, in "An Embarrassment of Bitches", a [[List of Castle episodes#Season 4 (2011–12)|season-four episode]] of ABC's ''[[Castle (TV series)|Castle]]''.{{cite web|title=Ep 13 – An Embarrassment of Bitches|url=http://castletv.net/ep-13-an-embarrassment-of-bitches|date=December 1, 2011|publisher=Castle TV on ABC & TNT|access-date=November 1, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120915235756/http://castletv.net/ep-13-an-embarrassment-of-bitches/|archive-date=September 15, 2012|url-status=dead}} 2024 saw the publication of her book, "Star Trek: Open a Channel: A Woman's Trek", a look at the female characters of the Star Trek franchise, and the actors who portrayed them. ==Personal life== [[File:Nana Visitor by Gage Skidmore.jpg|thumb|Nana Visitor at the 2018 [[WonderCon]]]] Visitor was married to Nick Miscusi from 1989 to 1994.{{cite web|last=Lipton |first = Michael A.|url=http://www.people.com/people/archive/article/0,,20106069,00.html|title=Winner by a Nose|date=August 16, 1993|newspaper=[[People (magazine)|People]]|volume=40|number=7}} They have one son together.{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e0fN_VBIn8w |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211212/e0fN_VBIn8w| archive-date=2021-12-12 |url-status=live|title=TABNation PSA - Nana Visitor|first=James P. |last = Coree|date=18 May 2015|via=YouTube}}{{cbignore}} Visitor began dating her ''Star Trek: Deep Space Nine'' co-star [[Alexander Siddig]] and married him in June 1997. They divorced in April 2001. They also have a son together, and her pregnancy was incorporated into her character and the series storyline, beginning in the 1996 fourth season episode "[[Body Parts (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Body Parts]]".{{cite book |last1 = Erdmann |first1 = Terry J. |last2 = Block |first2 = Paula M. |title = Star Trek: Deep Space Nine Companion |publisher = [[Pocket Books]] |year = 2000 |pages = 351–352 }}{{cite web |url = http://www.startrek.com/database_article/body-parts |title = Body Parts |work = StarTrek.com |access-date = August 12, 2013 }} She gave birth to her son on September 16, 1996, during production of the episode "[[The Assignment (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|The Assignment]]", though her character would remain pregnant until the fifth-season episode "[[The Begotten]]".{{harvp|Erdmann|Block|2000|p= 407|ps=.}} In early 2002, Visitor became engaged to Matthew Rimmer, previously company manager for the musical ''Chicago,'' and from 2017 chief operating officer of The Broad Stage in [[Santa Monica, California|Santa Monica]].{{cite web |title=Matthew Rimmer - Chief Operating Officer at BroadStage |url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthew-rimmer-a6196525?original_referer= |website=linkedin.com |publisher=Linkedin |access-date=8 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230208093423/https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthew-rimmer-a6196525?original_referer= |archive-date= 8 February 2023}}{{cite web |title=The Broad Stage Announces 2020/21 Season - '''René Marie Murat Auberjonois''' ({{IPAc-en|r|ə|ˈ|n|eɪ|_|oʊ|ˌ|b|ɛər|ʒ|ən|ˈ|w|ɑː}} {{respell|rə|NAY|_|oh|BAIR|zhən|WAH}};<ref>{{YouTube|lGnDakkxZCQ|Video Greeting from Rene Auberjonois}}</ref> June 1, 1940 – December 8, 2019) was an American actor. He was a [[Tony Awards|Tony Award]] and [[Drama Desk Awards|Drama Desk Award]] winner, and a three-time [[Emmy Awards|Emmy Award]] (two [[Primetime Emmy Awards|Primetime]], one [[Daytime Emmy Awards|Daytime]]) nominee, among other accolades.

He first achieved fame as a stage actor, winning the [[Tony Award for Best Featured Actor in a Musical]] in 1970 for his portrayal of Sebastian Baye opposite [[Katharine Hepburn]] in the [[André Previn]]–[[Alan Jay Lerner]] musical ''[[Coco (musical)|Coco]]''. He went on to earn three more Tony nominations for performances in [[Neil Simon]]'s ''[[The Good Doctor (play)|The Good Doctor]]'' (1973), [[Roger Miller]]'s ''[[Big River (musical)|Big River]]'' (1985), and [[Cy Coleman]]'s ''[[City of Angels (musical)|City of Angels]]'' (1989); he won a [[Drama Desk Award]] for ''Big River''. In 2018, Auberjonois was inducted into the [[American Theater Hall of Fame]].<ref name=":0"/>

A screen actor with more than 200 credits, Auberjonois was most famous for portraying characters in the main casts of several long-running television series, including Clayton Endicott III on ''[[Benson (TV series)|Benson]]'' (1980–86), for which he was an Emmy nominee; [[Odo (Star Trek)|Odo]] on ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' (1993–99), and [[Paul Lewiston]] on ''[[Boston Legal]]'' (2004–08). In films, Auberjonois appeared in several [[Robert Altman]] productions, notably [[List of M*A*S*H characters#Father John Mulcahy|Father John Mulcahy]] in the film version of ''[[M*A*S*H (film)|M*A*S*H]]'' (1970); the expedition scientist Roy Bagley in ''[[King Kong (1976 film)|King Kong]]'' (1976); Chef Louis in ''[[The Little Mermaid (1989 film)|The Little Mermaid]]'' (1989), in which he sang "[[Les Poissons]]"; and Reverend Oliver in ''[[The Patriot (2000 film)|The Patriot]]'' (2000). Auberjonois also performed as a voice actor in several video games, most notable being his role as Mr. Robert Edwin House, the reclusive Las Vegas casino owner in ''[[Fallout: New Vegas]]'' (2010).

== Early life and education ==
René Marie Murat Auberjonois was born June 1, 1940, in [[Manhattan]], New York City.<ref name="NYTO">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/08/obituaries/rene-auberjonois-dead.html|title=René Auberjonois, a 'Deep Space Nine' Star, Dies at 79|newspaper=The New York Times|date=December 8, 2019|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191209001004/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/08/obituaries/rene-auberjonois-dead.html|archive-date=December 9, 2019|last=Genzlinger|first=Neil|author-link=Neil Genzlinger}}</ref> His father, Swiss-born [[Fernand Auberjonois]], was a [[Cold War]]–era foreign correspondent and [[Pulitzer Prize]]–nominated writer. Auberjonois' mother, Princess Laure Louise Napoléone Eugénie Caroline Murat, was a great-great-granddaughter of [[Joachim Murat]] (one of [[Napoleon]]'s [[Marshal of the Empire|marshals]] and [[Kingdom of Naples|King of Naples]] during the [[First French Empire]]), and his wife—Napoleon's youngest sister—[[Caroline Bonaparte]]. Auberjonois had a sister and a brother, and two half-sisters from his mother's first marriage.<ref>{{Cite news| url=http://www.postgazette.com/pg/04241/369197.stm| title=Obituary: Fernand Auberjonois/Much admired foreign correspondent who lived a chronicle of 20th century| newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]| date=August 28, 2004| first=Jack| last=Lessenberry| agency=Block News Alliance| access-date=November 2, 2019| archive-date=January 22, 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090122213236/http://www.postgazette.com/pg/04241/369197.stm| url-status=dead}}</ref> Auberjonois wrote that his French family name, an uncommon one in the United States, means "[[armorer]]."<ref>{{Cite web| url=https://renefiles.com/facts-biography/rene-answers-your-questions/trek/| title=Trek Questions |website= renefiles.com| access-date=November 2, 2019}}</ref>

Auberjonois' grandfather, also named [[René Auberjonois (painter)|René Auberjonois]], was a Swiss [[post-Impressionist]] painter. His maternal grandmother, Hélène Macdonald Stallo, was an American from [[Cincinnati]], Ohio; his maternal grandfather's mother was a Russian noblewoman, Eudoxia Michailovna Somova, and his maternal grandfather's paternal grandmother, Caroline Georgina Fraser, who was the wife of [[Prince Napoleon Lucien Charles Murat]], was a Scottish American from [[Charleston, South Carolina]].

Auberjonois' family moved to Paris after [[World War II]]. After a few years in France, the family moved back to the United States and joined the [[South Mountain Road]] artists' colony in [[Rockland County, New York]], whose residents included [[Burgess Meredith]], [[John Houseman]], and [[Lotte Lenya]].<ref>{{Cite court | litigants=New York Trap Rock Corp. v. The Town of Clarkstown et al.| reporter=NY 272 App. Div.| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x83ffjFYLB4C| opinion=1021| court=Appellate Division, Supreme Court of New York, Second Department| date=May 11, 1955| access-date=December 9, 2019}}</ref>

The Auberjonois family also lived for a time in London, where Auberjonois completed high school while studying theater.<ref name="Rawson">{{Cite news| title=Theater Hall of Fame inductee Rene Auberjonois has Pittsburgh ties| url=https://www.post-gazette.com/ae/theater-dance/2018/11/16/Theater-Hall-of-Fame-inductee-Rene-Auberjonois-has-Pittsburgh-ties/stories/201811160111| date=November 16, 2018| newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]| last=Rawson| first=Christopher| access-date= December 9, 2019}}</ref> To complete his education, he attended the Carnegie Institute of Technology (now [[Carnegie Mellon University]]), and graduated with a Bachelor of Fine Arts from the College of Fine Arts in 1962.<ref>{{Cite journal| url= https://www.cmu.edu/cmnews/051001/051001_rene.html| journal=Carnegie Mellon News| date=May 10, 2001| title="Esteemed Group" Garners Honorary Degrees at 104th Commencement| quote= Called an 'actor's actor' by his peers, Auberjonois, a 1962 graduate of the School of Drama, earned many accolades for his performances in television, in film and on Broadway during his 40-year career.| access-date=November 2, 2019}}</ref>

== Career ==
=== Theater ===
After college, Auberjonois worked with several different theater companies, beginning with three years at the prestigious [[Arena Stage]] in Washington, D.C. Auberjonois later stated that the school was his unofficial graduate school.<ref name="Rawson"/> He traveled between Los Angeles, California, and New York, working in numerous theater productions. He helped found Bill Ball's [[American Conservatory Theater]] in Pittsburgh, playing the title roles in both "[[Tartuffe]]" and "[[King Lear]]," before moving with the company to San Francisco. Then came the [[Mark Taper Forum]] in Los Angeles, and the [[Brooklyn Academy of Music]] Repertory Company in New York City. He was a member of the [[Peninsula Players]] summer theater program during the 1962 season.<ref>Peninsula Players 65th Anniversary Program, 1999</ref>

Auberjonois was a member of the original faculty of the [[Juilliard School]]'s Drama Division when it opened in 1968 under [[John Houseman]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Farah |date=September 14, 2007 |title=Juilliard Drama Division Opens (1968) |url=https://journal.juilliard.edu/journal/juilliard-drama-division-opens-1968 |work=Juilliard Journal|first=Jeni Dahmus}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Kathleen |date=December 9, 2019 |title=Remembering René Auberjonois |url=https://www.geekscape.net/remembering-rene-auberjonois |website=Geekscape|first=Deidra}}</ref>

In 1968, Auberjonois landed a role on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]], and appeared in three plays that season: as Fool to [[Lee J. Cobb]]'s ''[[King Lear]]'' (the longest running production of the play in Broadway history), as Ned in ''[[A Cry of Players]]'' (which played in repertory with ''King Lear'') opposite [[Frank Langella]], and as Marco in ''Fire!'' In 1969, he earned a [[Tony Award]] for his performance as Sebastian Baye alongside [[Katharine Hepburn]] in ''[[Coco (musical)|Coco]]''.<ref name="tony-db">{{Cite web| title=Tony Awards Database: René Auberjonois| url=http://www.tonyawards.com/p/tonys_search?start=0&year=&award=&lname=Ren%E9+Auberjonois&fname=&show=| publisher=American Theatre Wing| access-date=January 29, 2008| archive-date=January 23, 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090123174949/http://www.tonyawards.com/p/tonys_search?start=0&year=&award=&lname=Ren%E9+Auberjonois&fname=&show=| url-status=dead}}</ref>

He received Tony nominations for his roles in [[Neil Simon]]'s ''[[The Good Doctor (play)|The Good Doctor]]'' (1973) opposite [[Christopher Plummer]]; as the Duke in ''[[Big River (musical)|Big River]]'' (1984), winning a [[Drama Desk Award]]; and, memorably, as Buddy Fidler/Irwin S. Irving in ''[[City of Angels (musical)|City of Angels]]'' (1989), written by [[Larry Gelbart]] and [[Cy Coleman]].<ref name="tony-db"/>

Auberjonois' other [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] appearances included Malvolio in ''[[Twelfth Night]]'' (1972); Scapin in ''Tricks'' (1973); Mr. Samsa in ''[[The Metamorphosis|Metamorphosis]]'' (1989); Professor Abronsius in ''[[Dance of the Vampires (musical)|Dance of the Vampires]]'', the English-language version of [[Jim Steinman]]'s musical adaptation of ''Tanz der Vampire''; and Jethro Crouch in ''[[Sly Fox]]'' (2004), for which he was nominated for Outstanding Featured Actor in a Play, an [[Outer Critics Circle Award]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.playbill.com/article/outer-critics-circle-award-nominations-announced-wicked-soars-with-10-com-119162|title=Outer Critics Circle Award Nominations Announced; Wicked Soars with 10|last=Ernio |first=Hernandez |date=April 18, 2004|website=Playbill|access-date=December 24, 2019}}</ref>

Auberjonois appeared many times at the [[Mark Taper Forum]], notably as [[Malvolio]] in ''Twelfth Night'' and as [[Stanislavski]] in ''Chekhov in Yalta''. As a member of the Second Drama Quartet,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Woodard|first=Josef|title=Theater: The Second Drama Quartet Follows in Famous Footsteps : It reprises a 'Don Juan in Hell' acclaimed when done by Charles Laughton, Tyrone Power and Agnes Moorehead. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-04-28-vl-51435-story.html |website=Los Angeles Times |access-date=December 9, 2019 |date=April 28, 1994}}</ref> he toured with [[Ed Asner]], [[Dianne Wiest]], and [[Harris Yulin]]. He appeared in the [[Tom Stoppard]] and [[André Previn]] work, ''[[Every Good Boy Deserves Favour (play)|Every Good Boy Deserves Favor]]'', at the [[John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts]] in Washington, D.C., and the [[Metropolitan Opera]] in New York.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Gussow |first=Mel |date=July 31, 1979 |title=Theater: Stoppard's 'Every Good Boy' |pages=C8 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/120793056 |url-access=subscription |access-date=September 14, 2023 |id={{ProQuest|120793056}} |author-link=Mel Gussow}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=McLellan |first=Joseph |date=August 8, 1979 |title=Deja-Vu Brilliance: 'EGBDF,' the Second Time Around |pages=E1, E9 |newspaper=The Washington Post|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/147189876 |url-access=subscription |access-date=September 14, 2023 |id={{ProQuest|147189876}}}}</ref>

He directed many theatrical productions, and starred in the Washington, D.C. production of ''[[Twelve Angry Men (1964 play)|12 Angry Men]]'' (2004), where he portrayed "Juror #5" to [[Roy Scheider]]'s "#8" and [[Robert Prosky]]'s "#3". He made his debut at the [[Shakespeare Theatre Company]] in Washington, D.C., in 2008 as the titular character in [[Molière]]'s ''[[The Imaginary Invalid]]''.

He was on the advisory board of [[Sci-Fest LA]], the first annual Los Angeles Science Fiction One-Act Play Festival, held in May 2014.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Sci-Fest Team| url=http://www.sci-fest.com/#!team/c1a9y| access-date=January 26, 2014| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181204013945/http://www.sci-fest.com/#!team/c1a9y| archive-date=December 4, 2018| url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2018, Auberjonois was inducted into the [[American Theater Hall of Fame]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/ae/theater-dance/2018/11/16/2018-Theater-Hall-of-Fame-inductees-Rene-Auberjonois-Christine-Baranski-Cicely-Tyson/stories/201811160109 |title=2018 Theater Hall of Fame inductees include Rene Auberjonois, Christine Baranski, Cicely Tyson and more |last=Rawson |first=Christopher |date=November 16, 2018 |work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |access-date=December 26, 2018}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=René Auberjonois – Broadway Cast & Staff {{!}} IBDB |url=https://www.ibdb.com/broadway-cast-staff/ren-auberjonois-66778#Awards |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=ibdb.com}}</ref>

=== Films ===
Auberjonois played Father Mulcahy in the original film version of ''[[M*A*S*H (film)|M*A*S*H]]''. His subsequent film roles included the gangster Tony in ''[[Police Academy 5: Assignment Miami Beach]]'' (1988), and Reverend Oliver in ''[[The Patriot (2000 film)|The Patriot]]'' (2000). He made [[cameo appearance]]s in a number of films, including a mental asylum doctor patterned after [[Tim Burton]], in ''[[Batman Forever]]'' (1995), and a bird expert who gradually transforms into a bird in [[Robert Altman]]'s 1970 film ''[[Brewster McCloud]]''. He appeared as Colonel West, a minor role in the 1991 ''[[Star Trek]]'' film ''[[Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country]]'', but his part was cut from the theatrical release. His other notable film appearances include: ''[[McCabe & Mrs. Miller]]'' (1971), ''[[Images (film)|Images]] ''(1972), ''[[Pete 'n' Tillie]]'' (1972), ''[[The Hindenburg (film)|The Hindenburg]]'' (1975), ''[[King Kong (1976 film)|King Kong]]'' (1976), ''[[The Big Bus]]'' (1976), ''[[Eyes of Laura Mars]]'' (1978), ''[[Where the Buffalo Roam]]'' (1980), ''[[Walker (film)|Walker]]'' (1987), ''[[My Best Friend Is a Vampire]]'' (1987), ''The Feud'' (1989), ''[[Inspector Gadget (film)|Inspector Gadget]]'' (1999), and ''[[Eulogy (film)|Eulogy]]'' (2004).

Auberjonois portrayed the character of Straight Hollander in the 1993 [[Miramax]] film ''[[The Ballad of Little Jo]]''. He voiced [[Professor Genius]] in ''[[Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland]]'', [[List of The Little Mermaid characters#Chef Louis|Louis the Chef]] in ''[[The Little Mermaid (franchise)|The Little Mermaid]]'' franchise, Flanagan in ''[[Cats Don't Dance]]'', the Butler in ''[[Joseph: King of Dreams]]'', and André in ''[[Planes: Fire & Rescue]]''.

In 2019, Auberjonois portrayed the title role in ''[[Raising Buchanan]]'' as U.S. president [[James Buchanan]].

=== Television ===
[[File:Shimerman, Visitor and Auberjonois by Beth Madison, 2.jpg|thumb|Auberjonois (right) with ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' co-stars [[Armin Shimerman]] (left) and [[Nana Visitor]] (center)]]
In addition to having been a regular actor on three television shows (''[[Benson (TV series)|Benson]]'', a situation comedy; ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' in science fiction; and ''[[Boston Legal]]'', a [[legal drama|legal]] [[comedy drama]]), Auberjonois guest starred on many television series, including; ''[[Nash Bridges]]'', ''[[Ellery Queen]]'', ''[[Family (1976 TV series)|Family]]'', ''[[Grey's Anatomy]]'', ''[[The Rockford Files]]'', ''[[Charlie's Angels]]'', ''[[Starsky & Hutch]]'', ''[[Wonder Woman (TV series)|Wonder Woman]]'', ''[[Harry O]]'', ''[[The Jeffersons]]'', ''[[The Outer Limits (1995 TV series)|The Outer Limits]]'', ''[[Night Gallery]]'', ''[[Hart to Hart]]'', ''[[Matlock (1986 TV series)|Matlock]]'', ''[[Murder, She Wrote]]'', ''[[The Bionic Woman]]'', ''[[Frasier]]'', ''[[Judging Amy]]'', ''[[Chicago Hope]]'', ''[[The Bob Newhart Show]]'', ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'', ''[[Stargate SG-1]]'', ''[[Warehouse 13]]'', ''[[Archer (2009 TV series)|Archer]]'', ''[[L.A. Law]]'', ''[[The Practice]]'' (for which he received an Emmy nomination, playing a different character than the one he played on ''The Practice'' spinoff ''Boston Legal''), ''[[Saving Grace (American TV series)|Saving Grace]]'', ''[[It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia]]'', ''[[Criminal Minds]]'', ''[[NCIS (TV series)|NCIS]]'', ''[[The Good Wife]]'', ''[[The Librarians (2014 TV series)|The Librarians]]'', and ''[[Madam Secretary (TV series)|Madam Secretary]]''.

His television film credits include ''[[The Rhinemann Exchange]]'', ''[[The Dark Secret of Harvest Home]]'', Disney's ''[[Geppetto (film)|Geppetto]]'', [[Gore Vidal]]'s ''Billy The Kid'', the remake of ''A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court'', and the ''Sally Hemings: An American Scandal'' (2000) miniseries. He portrayed the character [[The Cask of Amontillado|Fortunato]] in an episode of ''[[American Masters]]'' entitled "[[Edgar Allan Poe|Edgar Allan Poe: Terror of the Soul]]" (1995). He received a third Emmy Award nomination for his performance in ABC's ''The Legend of Sleepy Hollow''. He played NASA scientist Dr. Felix Blackwell in the ''[[NCIS (TV series)|NCIS]]'' episode "Phoenix".

[[File:Odo.jpg|thumb|Auberjonois as Odo in ''Star Trek: Deep Space Nine'']]Auberjonois directed television shows, including ''[[Marblehead Manor]]'', and various episodes of ''Deep Space Nine''.

=== Voice acting ===
[[File:Rene Auberjonois by Luigi Rosa, 11.jpg|thumb|upright|Pictured in 2010]]
Auberjonois was active in radio drama. He read "The Stunt" by Mordechai Strigler for the [[National Public Radio]] (NPR) series ''Jewish Stories From the Old World to the New'', and he recorded novels on tape. On [[Public Radio International|PRI]], he was featured numerous times on ''[[Selected Shorts]]'', reading works of dramatic fiction. His voice was heard in Disney's ''[[The Little Mermaid (1989 film)|The Little Mermaid]]'' (in the supporting role of Chef Louis, singing "Les Poissons").

He did voice work on the ''Challenge of the GoBots'' series in 1980s as Dr. Braxis and was the voice of Peter Parker on the 1972 [[Buddah Records]] [[Spider-Man]] LP "From Beyond the Grave" (BDS 5119), a radio-style narrative replete with sound effects and rock and roll song interludes.

He voice acted in ''[[The Last Unicorn (film)|The Last Unicorn]]'' as the Skull that guards the clock that serves as an entryway into the Red Bull's lair. [[Peter S. Beagle]], the author of the [[The Last Unicorn|original book]], praised Auberjonois' performance, saying "he could have played any role in that movie and I would have been happy ... He's that talented."

In 1984–1985, Auberjonois voiced [[DeSaad]] in the animated series ''[[Super Friends]]''. From 1986 to 1987, he voiced Alvinar in the series ''[[Wildfire (1986 TV series)|Wildfire]]''.

He provided the voice for Janos Audron, an ancient vampire in the ''[[Legacy of Kain]]'' video game series; he was in ''[[Soul Reaver 2]]'', ''[[Blood Omen 2]]'', and ''[[Legacy of Kain: Defiance]]''. He provided the voice of Angler in the ''[[Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End (video game)|Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End]]'' video game. He voiced [[General Zod]] in the [[Ruby-Spears]] animated ''[[Superman (TV series)|Superman]]'' series episode "The Hunter".

Auberjonois provided minor character voices for ''[[Justice League (TV series)|Justice League]]'', reprising his role as DeSaad and voicing [[Kanjar Ro]] and [[Galius Zed]].

Auberjonois lent his voice talents to the 2001 Public Broadcasting System (PBS) ''[[American Experience]]'' documentary "Woodrow Wilson" as the title character, along with the 2003 PBS historical documentary ''[[Kingdom of David: The Saga of the Israelites]]''.

In 2003, he provided the voice of Natori in the English dubbed version of semi-sequel to the [[Hayao Miyazaki]] film ''[[Whisper of the Heart]]'', ''[[The Cat Returns]]''. He reprised an animated version of his character [[Odo (Star Trek)|Odo]] from ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' in a cutaway joke in ''[[Family Guy]]''{{'}}s ''[[Stewie Griffin: The Untold Story]]''. The cutaway featured a more humanoid-faced Odo threatening [[Stewie Griffin|Stewie]]'s alleged cousin [[Quark (Star Trek)|Quark]]. Auberjonois also lent his voice to ''[[Skylanders: SuperChargers]]''.

In 2011, he voiced villain [[Blockbuster (DC Comics)|Mark Desmond]] in [[Cartoon Network]]'s ''[[Young Justice (TV series)|Young Justice]]''. He was also the voice of Leonard McLeish and Junkyard Jim in the ''[[Pound Puppies (2010 TV series)|Pound Puppies]]'' series, [[Pepé Le Pew]] in ''[[The Looney Tunes Show]]'', [[Azmuth]] in ''[[Ben 10: Omniverse]]'', and [[Ebony Maw]] in ''[[Avengers Assemble (TV series)|Avengers Assemble]]''.<ref name="btva">{{cite web |title=Rene Auberjonois (visual voices guide) |url=http://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/Rene-Auberjonois/ |access-date=September 23, 2023 |website=Behind the Voice Actors}} A green check mark indicates that a role has been confirmed using a screenshot (or collage of screenshots) of a title's list of voice actors and their respective characters found in its credits or other reliable sources of information.</ref>

==== Video games ====
{{More citations needed|date=December 2019}}
One of Auberjonois' earliest forays into video game voice acting was the role of Janos Audron in ''[[Soul Reaver 2]]''; he continued to voice the character in subsequent releases in the ''[[Legacy of Kain]]'' series. According to a behind-the-scenes featurette in ''Soul Reaver 2'', showing candid discussions among the voice actors during recording, he was surprised at the quality of the writing, asking, "This is for a video game?!" when the purpose of the recordings was brought to light.

Auberjonois provided the voice of [[List of Uncharted characters#Karl Schäfer|Karl Schäfer]], the honorable German explorer in the video game ''[[Uncharted 2: Among Thieves]]'', and Mr. House, the reclusive New Vegas casino owner in the 2010 video game ''[[Fallout: New Vegas]]''. He also voiced Dr. Ignatio Mobius in ''[[Command & Conquer: Renegade]]''. He reprised his role as Odo in the game ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine: The Fallen]]''. In June 2018 he reprised his role as Odo in the [[massively multiplayer online role-playing game]] ''[[Star Trek Online]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.arcgames.com/en/games/star-trek-online/news/detail/10838844-victory-is-life-our-fourth-expansion,-coming-june-2018! |title=Victory Is Life – Our Fourth Expansion, Coming June 2018! |website=March 21, 2018 |publisher=Perfect World Entertainment |access-date=November 26, 2018}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Auberjonois was married to Judith Helen Mihalyi from 1963 until his death in 2019. They had a daughter, Tessa,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Robin |first=Brian |date=February 21, 2023 |title=Leaping into Her Father's Advice |url=https://www.scr.org/scr-blog/posts/leaping-into-her-father-s-advice/ |access-date=October 2, 2025 |website=South Coast Repertory}}</ref> and a son, [[Remy Auberjonois|Rèmy-Luc]],<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/rene-auberjonois-died-beson-star-trek-deep-space-nine-actor-dead-age-79-cause-of-death-metastatic-lung-cancer/ |title=René Auberjonois, "Benson," "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" actor, has died at age 79 |date=December 9, 2019 |publisher=CBS News |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> both of whom also became actors.

=== Illness and death ===
In an interview with ''[[Compassion & Choices]] Magazine'', Judith Auberjonois revealed that René Auberjonois underwent chemotherapy for lung cancer in 2018. It was discovered in 2019 that the cancer had spread to his brain. Due to the potential for [[Radiation-induced cognitive decline|serious cognitive side effects]], Auberjonois chose not to pursue the [[whole-brain radiation]] treatment suggested by his doctors.<ref name="CompassionChoicesMagazine">{{cite magazine |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=Five Questions for Judith Auberjonois |url=https://compassionandchoices.org/docs/default-source/magazine/2021-summer-magazine-online-final.pdf?sfvrsn=23f52545_1 |magazine=Compassion & Choices Magazine|pages=18–20 |date=Summer 2021 |access-date=February 6, 2022}}</ref>

As a resident of California, Auberjonois decided to seek [[Assisted suicide in the United States|medical aid in dying]] under the [[California End of Life Option Act]].<ref name="CompassionChoicesMagazine"/><ref name="CTPostAidInDying">{{cite news |last=Tucker |first=Michael |date=February 19, 2021 |title=Opinion: Actor explains how medical aid in dying bill can provide comfort |url=https://www.ctpost.com/opinion/article/Opinion-Actor-explains-how-medical-aid-in-dying-15961624.php |work=Connecticut Post |location=Bridgeport, CT |access-date=February 6, 2022 |archive-date=October 13, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221013031734/https://www.ctpost.com/opinion/article/Opinion-Actor-explains-how-medical-aid-in-dying-15961624.php |url-status=dead }}</ref> On December 6, 2019, he spent his final hours with his family at his home in Los Angeles reminiscing over photos and listening to music.<ref name="CTPostAidInDying"/> He then took the medication prescribed for assisted suicide and died two days later at the age of 79. The California End of Life Option Act stipulates that death certificates should list the underlying terminal illness as the cause of death, rather than the use of life-ending medications.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tinker |first1=Ben |title=111 people died under California's new right-to-die law |url=https://www.cnn.com/2017/06/28/health/california-end-of-life-2016-bn/index.html |publisher=CNN|access-date=February 6, 2022 |date=June 29, 2017}}</ref> His cause of death was given as [[metastatic]] lung cancer.<ref name=NYTO/><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/benson-star-trek-actor-rene-auberjonois-has-died-at-79/2019/12/08/db319e26-1a05-11ea-977a-15a6710ed6da_story.html |title='Benson,' 'Star Trek' actor René Auberjonois has died at 79 |first=Andrew |last=Dalton |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=December 8, 2019 |access-date=December 8, 2019}}</ref>

{{marriage|Becky Hopkins|1999}} | children = 1 }} '''Gary Rand Graham''' (June 6, 1950 – January 22, 2024) was an American actor. With a career spanning five decades beginning in the 1970s in television and movies, he is perhaps best known for his starring role as Detective Matthew Sikes in the television series ''[[Alien Nation (TV series)|Alien Nation]]'' (1989–1990) and five subsequent ''Alien Nation'' television films (1994–1997), as well as his work in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise, most notably the recurring role of [[Soval]], the [[Vulcan (Star Trek)|Vulcan]] ambassador to Earth in ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]''. == Biography and early career == Graham was born in [[Long Beach, California]]. One of his earliest roles was in the 1980 [[CBS]] miniseries ''[[Scruples (miniseries)|Scruples]]'', based on the [[Judith Krantz]] novel starring [[Lindsay Wagner]]. He was cast as a hitman on the television show ''[[Moonlighting (TV series)|Moonlighting]]'' co-starring opposite [[Bruce Willis]]. Graham played more than 38 TV roles and had been in more than 40 movies. As a musician, Graham was in the bands The Gary Graham Garage Band, The Gary Graham Band and The Sons of Kirk. Graham was also a contributor to [[Breitbart News]].{{Cite book |last=Cole |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jkMxCgAAQBAJ&pg=PT187 |title=Republican Party Animal: The "Bad Boy of Holocaust History" Blows the Lid off Hollywood's Secret Right-Wing Underground |date=May 19, 2014 |publisher=Feral House |isbn=978-1-936239-92-4}} Graham died from cardiac arrest in [[Spokane, Washington]] on January 22, 2024, at the age of 73.{{cite web|last=Barnes|first=Mike|title=Gary Graham, Star of 'Alien Nation,' Dies at 73|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/gary-graham-dead-alien-nation-1235804804/|website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=January 23, 2024|access-date=January 23, 2024}}{{cite news |last=Watters |first=Bill |date=January 22, 2024 |title=Gary Graham, Star of "Alien Nation", "Enterprise" Has Passed Away |url=https://nerdbot.com/2024/01/22/gary-graham-star-of-alien-nation-enterprise-has-passed-away/ |access-date=January 23, 2024 |publisher=Nerdbot}} ==Later career== === Television === Graham starred in a 2008 television pilot styled after ''[[Sin City]]'' called ''Dead End City''. He also appeared in the December 18, 1984 episode of ''[[Remington Steele]]'', "Let's Steele A Plot" (season 3, episode 11), as Butch Bemis. As well as starring as Detective Matthew Sikes in the television series ''[[Alien Nation (TV series)|Alien Nation]]'' (1989–1990), he resumed this role in the TV movies ''[[Alien Nation: Dark Horizon]]'' (1994), ''[[Alien Nation: Body and Soul]]'' (1995), ''[[Alien Nation: Millennium]]'' (1996), ''[[Alien Nation: The Enemy Within]]'' (1996) and ''[[Alien Nation: The Udara Legacy]]'' (1997). Graham starred on ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'' as the recurring character [[Ambassador Soval]], a [[Vulcan (Star Trek)|Vulcan]] [[Ambassador (diplomacy)|ambassador]] to Earth. He also guest-starred on ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'' (1995) once, playing [[Ocampa]]n community leader Tanis in the second-season episode "[[Cold Fire (Star Trek: Voyager)|Cold Fire]]". He played Ragnar in the fan production ''[[Star Trek: Of Gods and Men]]'' and continued that role in ''[[Star Trek: Renegades]]''. In 2015, Graham reprised his role as Ambassador Soval, in the [[fan film]] ''[[Star Trek: Axanar]]''.{{Cite web |last=Howell |first=Elizabeth |date=2015-07-10 |title='Star Trek: Axanar' Fan Film Kicks Fundraising into Warp Drive |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/star-trek-axanar-fan-film-kicks-fundraising-warp-171422536.html |access-date=2024-12-09 |website=Yahoo News |language=en-US}} === Film === Graham's film appearances include ''[[Hardcore (1979 film)|Hardcore]]'', ''[[The Hollywood Knights]]'', ''[[All the Right Moves (film)|All the Right Moves]]'', ''[[The Arrogant]]'', ''The Last Warrior'', ''[[Robot Jox]]'', ''Running Woman'' and ''Siren'' (2006). His most recent films are ''[[InAlienable]]'', ''Action Hero'' and ''[[Dreams Awake]]''. He made his directorial debut in the spring of 2008 with the film ''Interviews,'' which he also wrote. === Web-based work === Graham also made appearances as the "Smoking Jacket Guy" in the introduction and other scenes in the Internet gaming show ''[[The Jace Hall Show]]''.{{cite web|url=http://crackle.com/c/Jace_Hall#id=298717&ml=o%3D12%26fpl%3D297045%26fx%3D|title=Crackle - Watch Movies Online, Free TV Shows, & Original Online Series}} Graham played Dr. David Macavoy in the web series ''Universal Dead''.{{cite web|url=http://www.universaldead.com/ |title=Universal Dead |publisher=Universal Dead |access-date=2012-06-04}} In late June 2010, it was announced that ''Universal Dead'' will be made into a feature film. It never was, as of 2026.{{cite web|url=http://indieintertube.tv/static/universal-dead-full-length-feature|title=Universal Dead full length feature?|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110818124246/http://indieintertube.tv/static/universal-dead-full-length-feature/|archive-date=2011-08-18}} ==Filmography== ===Film=== {| class="wikitable sortable" |- ! [[University of Washington]] ([[Bachelor of Fine Arts|BFA]]) | occupation = Actor | years_active = 1971–present | spouse = Alice Cadogan{{cite web |title= - 17th July 1996 Actor Jeffrey Combs and wife Alice Cadogan -|url=https://www.alamy.com/universal-city-california-usa-17th-july-1996-actor-jeffrey-combs-and-wife-alice-cadogan-attend-universal-pictures-the-frighteners-premiere-at-cineplex-odeon-universal-city-cinemas-on-july-17-1996-in-universal-city-california-usa-photo-by-barry-kingalamy-stock-photo-image554643364.html |website=alamy.com |publisher=[[Alamy]] |access-date=19 December 2025}}{{cite web |title=Jeffrey Combs... and wife Alice attend the "Star Trek: Enterprise" Finale Party ...April 13, 2005 |url=https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/actor-jeffrey-combs-and-wife-alice-attend-the-star-trek-news-photo/52628134 |website=gettyimages.com |publisher=[[Getty Images]] |access-date=19 December 2025}} }} '''Jeffrey Alan Combs''' (born September 9, 1954) is an American actor. He is best known for starring as [[Herbert West]] in the [[H.P. Lovecraft]] adaptation ''[[Re-Animator]]'' (1985) and portraying a number of characters in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' universe, most notably [[Liquidator Brunt|Brunt]] and the various [[List of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine characters#Weyoun|Weyouns]] on ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' (1994–1999), and [[List of Star Trek: Enterprise characters#Thy'lek Shran|Shran]] on ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'' (2001–2005). Combs has been a prominent figure within the [[horror film|horror genre]] through most of his career, acting in eight films directed by ''Re-Animator'' director [[Stuart Gordon]] such as ''[[From Beyond (film)|From Beyond]]'' (1986), ''[[The Pit and the Pendulum (1991 film)|The Pit and the Pendulum]]'' (1991), and ''[[Castle Freak]]'' (1995). Other horror film appearances include ''[[Necronomicon (film)|Necronomicon]]'' (1993), [[Peter Jackson]]'s ''[[The Frighteners]]'' (1996), ''[[I Still Know What You Did Last Summer]]'' (1998), ''[[House on Haunted Hill (1999 film)|House on Haunted Hill]]'' (1999), and ''[[Would You Rather (film)|Would You Rather]]'' (2012). As a voice actor, Combs is best known as the voice of [[Question (character)|Question]] on ''[[Justice League Unlimited]]'' (2004–2006) and Ratchet on ''[[Transformers: Prime]]'' (2010–2013).{{cite web|title=Jeffrey Combs|url=https://www.nytimes.com/movies/person/14373/Jeffrey-Combs/filmography|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402181008/http://www.nytimes.com/movies/person/14373/Jeffrey-Combs/filmography|url-status=dead|department=Movies & TV Dept.|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=2015|archive-date=April 2, 2015}} ==Early life== Combs was born in [[Oxnard, California]], the fifth of nine children{{cite web | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bQZduhlbM1A?t=483 | title=Shuttlepod Episode 004: "That's Shrantastic!" with Jeffrey Combs | website=[[YouTube]] |last1=The Shuttlepod Show |date=Mar 13, 2022 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230927160731/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bQZduhlbM1A |archive-date= Sep 27, 2023 }} born to Jean Owens (formerly Sullins; 1921–1986) and Eugene "Gene" Combs (1922–1999), and raised in [[Lompoc, California|Lompoc]]. Both of his parents were from the [[Ozarks]] region of [[Arkansas]].{{cite web | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bQZduhlbM1A?t=473 | title=Shuttlepod Episode 004: "That's Shrantastic!" with Jeffrey Combs | website=[[YouTube]] |last1=The Shuttlepod Show |date=Mar 13, 2022 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230927160731/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bQZduhlbM1A |archive-date= Sep 27, 2023 }} A graduate of [[Lompoc High School]], as a senior, Combs played the lead role of Captain Fisby in a stage production of ''[[The Teahouse of the August Moon (play)|The Teahouse of the August Moon]]''. Combs then attended [[Santa Maria, California|Santa Maria]]'s [[Pacific Conservatory of the Performing Arts]] at [[Allan Hancock College]], and later developed his acting skills in the [[University of Washington School of Drama#Acting|Professional Actor's Training Program]] at the [[University of Washington]] from which he graduated in the late 1970s.{{Cite book|last=Olson|first=Christopher J.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yUdODwAAQBAJ&q=University+of+Washington+Jeffrey+Combs%3A&pg=PA186|title=100 Greatest Cult Films|date=April 12, 2018|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|isbn=978-1-4422-1104-9|language=en}} In 1980, after several years performing in playhouses on the [[West Coast of the United States|West Coast]], Combs moved to Los Angeles. He landed his first role in the film ''[[Honky Tonk Freeway]]'' (1981), playing an unnamed drive-in teller. His first horror film role came two years later in ''[[Frightmare (1981 film)|Frightmare]]'' (1983).{{Cite book|last=Rowan|first=Terry|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BjyyCQAAQBAJ&q=Frightmare+Jeffrey+Combs%3A&pg=PA36|title=The Book of the Undead A Zombie Film Guide|date=August 16, 2014 |publisher=Lulu.com|isbn=978-1-312-43947-4}}{{self-published source|date=May 2020}}{{self-published inline|date=February 2020}} ==Career== Combs's best-known horror role is [[Herbert West]], the main character in the film ''[[Re-Animator]]'' (1985),{{cite web|work=[[The New York Times]]|title=Re Animator (1985) SCREEN: STUART GORDON DIRECTS 'RE-ANIMATOR'|author-link=Janet Maslin|first=Janet|last=Maslin|date=October 18, 1985|url=https://www.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9E04EED91E39F93BA25753C1A963948260}} and its two sequels. He portrayed author [[H. P. Lovecraft]] (creator of the Herbert West character) in the film ''[[Necronomicon (film)|Necronomicon: Book of the Dead]]'' (1993) and has starred in eight adaptations of Lovecraft's works. Other film credits include ''The Attic Expeditions'' (2001), ''[[FeardotCom]]'' (2002), ''[[House on Haunted Hill (1999 film)|House on Haunted Hill]]'' (1999), ''[[I Still Know What You Did Last Summer]]'' (1998) and ''[[The Frighteners]]'' (1996).{{cite web| last=Mcivar| first=Brice| title=Q&A: Jeffrey Combs| url=http://www.fangoria.com/new/exclusive-qa-jeffrey-combs-on-motivational-growth/| work=[[The New York Times]]| date=August 9, 2011| access-date=August 9, 2011| archive-date=February 17, 2015| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150217235118/http://www.fangoria.com/new/exclusive-qa-jeffrey-combs-on-motivational-growth/| url-status=dead}} Combs has had roles in many science fiction television series. He starred as the telepath Harriman Gray in first-season episode "[[Eyes (Babylon 5)|Eyes]]" (1994) of ''[[Babylon 5]]''. In 2001, he played the sinister Dr. Ek in ''The Attic Expeditions''. In August 2005, he appeared for the first time on the science fiction series ''[[The 4400]]'' as [[Kevin Burkhoff|Dr. Kevin Burkhoff]] which became a recurring role by 2006. In early 2007, he played a highly fictionalized [[Edgar Allan Poe]] in "[[The Black Cat (Masters of Horror episode)|The Black Cat]]" episode of ''[[Masters of Horror]]''.[http://www.ugo.com/channels/filmtv/features/mastersofhorror/combs.asp Jeffrey Combs, Star of "The Black Cat"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080622075642/http://www.ugo.com/channels/filmTv/features/mastersofhorror/combs.asp |date=June 22, 2008 }}, [[UGO Networks|UGO]] In the 2012 miniseries ''[[Dorothy and the Witches of Oz]]'' (sometimes called ''The Witches of Oz''), he had a small role as a fictionalized version of [[L. Frank Baum]]. [[File:Jeffrey Combs (21268215296).jpg|thumb|upright|Combs in 2015]] Combs has also worked as a voiceover artist. His voiceover roles include the [[Scarecrow (DC Comics)|Scarecrow]] in ''[[The New Batman Adventures]]'', the [[Question (character)|Question]] in ''[[Justice League Unlimited]]'', Ratchet in ''[[Transformers: Prime]]'', the [[Leader (character)|Leader]] in ''[[The Avengers: Earth's Mightiest Heroes]]'', the [[Rat King (Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles)|Rat King]] in ''[[Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (2012 TV series)|Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles]]'', and [[Brainiac]] in ''[[Injustice 2]]''. He also narrated the 25th anniversary of ''[[Re-Animator]]'' at the [[Fantasia Festival|2010 FanTasia]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.dreadcentral.com/news/38586/fantasia-2010-days-5-9|title=Fantasia 2010: Days 5 Through 9|date=July 16, 2010 }} In July 2009, Combs returned to his stage roots and reprised his role as Edgar Allan Poe in a one-man theatrical show, ''Nevermore...an Evening with Edgar Allan Poe,'' at [[The Steve Allen Theater]] in Hollywood, California.[http://www.steveallentheater.com/nevermore Stebe Allen Theater – Nevermore] Although it was supposed to run for only a month, it enjoyed much success and sold-out crowds, and was extended four times, until closing in Los Angeles on December 19, 2009. The show had its East Coast debut on January 23 and 24, 2010 at Westminster Hall in Baltimore, Maryland, Poe's final resting place.[http://www.poebicentennial.com/events.html Baltimore Poe Bicentennial Celebration] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091228194129/http://poebicentennial.com/events.html |date=December 28, 2009 }} A tour of the Saturn Award-nominated{{Cite web|url=http://www.dreadcentral.com/news/38614/fantasia-2010-days-10-and-11|title=Fantasia 2010: Days 10 and 11|date=October 18, 2012}} ''Nevermore'' was subsequently planned.{{Cite web|url=http://www.dreadcentral.com/news/35577/nevermore-heading-san-diego-two-performances|title=Nevermore Heading to San Diego for Two Performances|date=July 18, 2012}} Combs starred with [[Andrew Divoff]] in the 2012 Screen Media Films release ''[[Night of the Living Dead 3D: Re-Animation]]'', a prequel to the 2006 film ''[[Night of the Living Dead 3D]]'' directed by [[Jeff Broadstreet]]. In 2012, he also played the sadistic Dr. Lambrick in another horror-thriller, ''[[Would You Rather (film)|Would You Rather]]''. ===''Star Trek''=== On television, Combs enjoyed popular success playing a number of alien characters on the various modern ''Star Trek'' incarnations, beginning with ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' in 1994, and continuing to ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'' in 2000, ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'' in 2001 and ''[[Star Trek: Lower Decks]]'' in 2021. He has played nine onscreen roles in the ''Star Trek'' universe. His largest science-fiction role to date was his regular guest role on ''Deep Space Nine'' as the [[Vorta]] clone [[Weyoun]]. Combs has said that Weyoun was his favorite ''Star Trek'' role, and that he had considerable input in developing the character.{{cite video |people=Jeffrey Combs |year=2004 |title=StarTrek.com First Person |url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FjA-hvKiCk0&feature=endscreen&NR=1 |publisher=Paramount Pictures |access-date=May 12, 2012}} On the same series, Combs had a recurring role as the [[Ferengi]] character [[List of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine characters#Brunt|Brunt]]. During the ''DS9'' episode "[[The Dogs of War (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|The Dogs of War]]", he appeared as both Weyoun and Brunt, becoming one of the few ''Star Trek'' actors to play two characters in the same episode (others including [[Patrick Stewart]], [[Brent Spiner]], and [[Brian Markinson]]).Peter Durst and Sulan, see [[Brian Markinson#Filmography|the Filmography section]]Jean-Luc Picard and Michael Williams, see ''[[The Defector (Star Trek: The Next Generation)|The Defector]]'' Combs wanted the characters to appear in the same scene, but the logistics and expense worked against it.{{cite web |title=Star Trek Online Community Q&A with Jeffrey Combs! |url=https://www.arcgames.com/de/games/xbox/star-trek-online/news/detail/10887074-community-q%2526a-with-jeffrey-combs%2521 |date=April 24, 2018 |access-date=May 13, 2020}} On ''Enterprise'', Combs had a recurring role as [[Shran]], an [[Andorian]] military officer. ''Enterprise'' producer [[Manny Coto]] once said in an interview that he had hoped to make Combs a regular on ''Enterprise'' had the series been renewed for a fifth season.{{cite web|url=http://trekmovie.com/2009/08/10/vegascon09-braga-coto-talk-enterprise-season-5-star-trek-2009-more/|last=Pascale|first=Anthony|title=VegasCon09: Braga & Coto Talk Enterprise Season 5 + Star Trek 2009 & more|publisher=[[TrekMovie.com]]|location=[[Las Vegas, Nevada]]|date=August 10, 2009|access-date=June 13, 2017}} In addition to his recurring ''Star Trek'' roles, Combs had non-recurring roles as human police officer Kevin Mulkahey,[http://www.startrek.com/database_article/far-beyond-the-stars Startrek.com Deep Space Nine – Far Beyond the Stars] alien Tiron on ''Deep Space Nine,'' alien [[Penk (Star Trek)|Penk]] on ''Voyager,'' and Ferengi pirate Krem on ''Enterprise''. Along with many other actors, writers and creators of the show, Combs also had a cameo appearance as a holographic patron in Vic's Lounge in the final episode of ''Deep Space Nine''. He also voices the character of Romulan Commander Suldok for the ''[[Star Trek: Elite Force II]]'' video game.{{Cite web |last=Webb |first=Andy |date=September 9, 2023 |title=Every Star Trek Character Played by Jeffrey Combs, Ranked |url=https://www.startrek.com/news/every-star-trek-character-played-by-jeffrey-combs-ranked |access-date=2025-07-04 |website=www.startrek.com |language=en}} In 2021, he had a guest voice role as AGIMUS, an evil computer, in episode 7, season 2 of ''[[Star Trek: Lower Decks]]'', which he reprised in seasons 3 and 4.{{Cite web |date=September 27, 2021 |title=Catching Up With Jeffrey Combs |url=https://www.startrek.com/news/catching-up-with-jeffrey-combs |access-date=2025-07-04 |website=www.startrek.com |language=en}} ==Filmography== ===Film=== {| class="wikitable sortable" |- ! {{short description|American actor (born 1956)}} {{Use American English|date=July 2026}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2026}} {{Infobox person | name = Tim Russ | image = Tim Russ by Gage Skidmore.jpg | caption = Russ at the 2022 [[Phoenix Fan Fusion]] | birth_name = Timothy Darrell Russ | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1956|6|22}} | birth_place = Washington, D.C., U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[St. Edward's University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Illinois State University]] (attended) | occupation = {{hlist|Actor|musician|screenwriter|producer|director}} | years_active = 1985–present | children = 1 }} '''Timothy Darrell Russ'''{{cite web| url= http://www.filmreference.com/film/92/Tim-Russ.html|title=Tim Russ Biography (1956-)|publisher= | website= filmreference.com}} (born June 22, 1956) is an American actor, musician, screenwriter, director and amateur astronomer. He is best known for his roles as [[Lieutenant Commander]] [[Tuvok]] on ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]''; [[Robert Johnson]] in ''[[Crossroads (1986 film)|Crossroads]]'' (1986); Casey in ''[[East of Hope Street]]'' (1998); Frank on ''[[Samantha Who?]]''; Principal Franklin on the [[Nickelodeon]] sitcom ''[[iCarly]]''; D. C. Montana on ''[[The Highwayman (TV series)|The Highwaymen]]'' (1987–1988), and for his brief role in ''[[Spaceballs]]'' (1987). He appeared in ''[[The Rookie: Feds]]'' (2022) and reprised his role as Captain Tuvok on Season 3 of ''[[Star Trek: Picard]]''. == Early life, family and education == Russ was born in Washington, D.C., on June 22, 1956, to a [[government employee]] mother and a [[U.S. Air Force]] officer father. He spent part of his childhood in [[Turkey]]. He attended his senior year of high school at [[Rome Free Academy]], from which he graduated in 1974.{{cite web|url= https://youtube.com/watch?v=W-vq-lJrXwM|title=Knight Time Interview w Tim Russ |date=January 21, 2021 | via= YouTube}} He graduated from [[St. Edward's University]] with a degree in theater arts. He additionally attended graduate school at [[Illinois State University]] where he was inducted into its Hall of Fame. With a girlfriend, Jedda Roskilly, he has a daughter.{{cite web |last1= Nausch|first1=Maria |title=Biographical notes |url=https://www.timrusstribute.com/Bio.htm |website=timrusstribute.com |access-date=April 20, 2026}} == Career == === Acting === In 1985, Russ appeared in ''[[The Twilight Zone (1985 TV series)|The Twilight Zone]]'' episodes "[[Kentucky Rye (The Twilight Zone)|Kentucky Rye]]" as Officer No. 2 and "[[Voices in the Earth (The Twilight Zone)|Voices in the Earth]]" as Archer. He made a brief appearance in the comedy film ''[[Spaceballs]]'' as a trooper who "combs" the desert with a giant comb.{{cite web |title=Clip of 'combing the desert', from the movie 'Spaceballs' | date= July 15, 2012| via= YouTube| url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g3iFJpGJiug}}{{cite web | url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0750913/?ref_=fn_al_nm_1 | title=Tim Russ | website=[[IMDb]] }} Russ had a prominent role in the Charles Bronson film ''[[Death Wish 4]].'' Russ has been involved in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise as a voice and film actor, writer, director, and producer. He played several minor roles before landing the role as the main character [[Tuvok]] in ''Star Trek: Voyager''. Russ screentested, in 1987, for the role of [[Geordi La Forge]] on ''Star Trek: The Next Generation'' before being cast as Tuvok. Russ went into ''Voyager'' as a dedicated [[Trekkie]] with an extensive knowledge of [[Vulcan (Star Trek)|Vulcan]] lore,{{cite web| url= http://www.ifmagazine.com/feature.asp?article=1726 | title= Set Report: iF Magazine Boldly Goes To Vulcan For Star Trek: Of Gods And Men| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090202091010/http://ifmagazine.com/feature.asp?article=1726 |archive-date= February 2, 2009| website= ifmagazine.com | publisher= }} and has played the following roles in the ''Star Trek'' universe: * Devor, a mercenary aboard the ''Enterprise-D'' disguised as a service engineer in ''The Next Generation'' episode "[[Starship Mine]]" (1993) * T'Kar, a [[Klingon]] in the ''Deep Space Nine'' episode "[[Invasive Procedures (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Invasive Procedures]]" (1993) * A human tactical Lieutenant on the USS ''Enterprise-B'' in the film ''[[Star Trek Generations]]'' (1994). * Tuvok's [[Mirror Universe]] counterpart in the ''Deep Space Nine'' episode "[[Through the Looking Glass (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Through the Looking Glass]]" (1995). * A changeling impersonating Tuvok in ''Star Trek: Picard'' season 3. In 1995, Russ co-wrote the story for the [[Malibu Comics]] ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' No. 29 and 30, with Mark Paniccia. Russ performed voice acting roles as Tuvok for the video games ''[[Star Trek: Voyager – Elite Force]]'' and ''[[Star Trek: Elite Force II]]''. Russ is the director and one of the stars of the fan series ''[[Star Trek: Of Gods and Men]]'', the first third of which was released in December 2007, with the remaining two-thirds released in 2008.{{Cite web |last=Administrator |title=Star Trek: Of Gods and Men |url=http://startrekofgodsandmen.com/main/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=58&Itemid=173 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081219182240/http://startrekofgodsandmen.com/main/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=58&Itemid=173 |archive-date=December 19, 2008 |access-date=September 30, 2025 |website=startrekofgodsandmen.com |language=en-gb}} Russ's character's name D. C. Montana in ''[[The Highwayman (TV series)|The Highwayman]]'' was a reference to ''Trek'' writer [[D. C. Fontana]].{{citation needed|date=June 2015}} In 1990, he appeared in an episode of ''[[Freddy's Nightmares]]''.{{Cite news|last1= Englund|first1=Robert|title=Dust to Dust|date= February 25, 1990|last2=Bergman|last3=Brestoff|last4=Dow|first2=Sandahl|first3=Richard|first4=Tony}}{{full citation needed|date=April 2019}} Russ directed and co-starred in ''[[Star Trek: Renegades]]'', and in both 2013 and 2014 reprised his role as the voice of Tuvok in the [[massively multiplayer online game]] ''[[Star Trek Online]]''.{{cite news |title=Star Trek producers and Voyager actor Tim Russ discuss Renegades| website= filmindustry.network |url= https://filmindustry.network/star-trek-producers-and-voyager-actor-tim-russ-discuss-renegades/18220 |publisher=Film Industry Network |date=November 17, 2012}} === Later work === [[File:Tim Russ (32382294283).jpg|thumb|Russ at the Paradise City Comic Con, December 2016]] Russ appeared as Frank, a sarcastic doorman in the sitcom ''[[Samantha Who?]]'' from 2007 to 2009, and appeared for six seasons as Principal Ted Franklin in [[Nickelodeon]]'s show ''[[iCarly]]''. He also portrayed a doctor on an episode of ''[[Hannah Montana]]'', "[[I Am Hannah, Hear Me Croak]]". Russ won an [[Emmy Award]] in 2014 for [[public service ad]]s he did for the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office on intellectual property theft and [[cyberbullying]].{{cite web|title=National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences Pacific Southwest Chapter 2014 Emmy Recipients List| url= http://nataspsw.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/2014-Recipient-List-for-Website.pdf| website= nataspsw.org| access-date= June 26, 2014}} He played Captain Kells in the 2015 [[Bethesda Game Studios]] video game ''[[Fallout 4]]''.{{cite web|url=https://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/video-games/Fallout-4/Lancer-Captain-Kells/|title=LANCER CAPTAIN KELLS|publisher=Behind the Voice Actors|access-date=April 26, 2021|archive-date=November 15, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151115060900/https://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/video-games/Fallout-4/Lancer-Captain-Kells/}} In June 2025, following [[Mel Brooks]]' announcement of ''Spaceballs 2'', slated for release in 2027, Russ teased on social media that he may appear in the film, along with his more famous co-stars.{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/movies/news/tim-russ-who-has-the-best-line-in-the-original-hints-at-spaceballs-2-return/ar-AA1GRGNE|title=MSN|website=Msn.com|access-date=July 29, 2026}} === Music and astronomy === Russ has been a lifelong musician and a singer.{{cite web|title=Tim Russ – Star Trek: Voyager's Tuvok|url=http://www.successcircuit.com/interviews/tim-russ/|publisher=Success Circuit|access-date=April 4, 2015|archivedate=April 8, 2015|url-status=usurped|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150408194420/http://www.successcircuit.com/interviews/tim-russ/}} In addition, Russ has been an avid amateur astronomer most of his adult life, and is a member of the Los Angeles Astronomical Society. In 2021 he was among a small group of citizen astronomers who assisted in detection of the asteroid [[617 Patroclus]] in preparation for [[NASA]]'s [[Lucy (spacecraft)|Lucy probe]].{{Cite news |last=Kochi |first=Sudiksha |date=August 27, 2021 |title='Star Trek' star Tim Russ helps detect asteroid for NASA's upcoming mission |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/2021/08/27/star-trek-actor-tim-russ-helps-nasa-detect-asteroid/8204195002/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230319050620/https://www.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/2021/08/27/star-trek-actor-tim-russ-helps-nasa-detect-asteroid/8204195002/ |archive-date=March 19, 2023 |access-date=January 27, 2024 |work=USA Today}} In February 2022, he stated that he owned a 10-inch Dobsonian telescope, an 8" Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope, and a Unistellar eVscope.{{Cite news |date=February 1, 2022 |title=Tim Russ: Actor, Director, and Amateur Astronomer |language=en-US |work=Sky & Telescope |url=https://skyandtelescope.org/astronomy-resources/famous-astronomers/tim-russ-actor-director-amateur-astronomer/#:~:text=Tim%20Russ%20is%20best%20known,Tuvok%20on%20Star%20Trek:%20Voyager. |access-date=February 20, 2023}} == Filmography == === Film === {| class="wikitable sortable" |+ {{Screen reader-only| Tim Russ film credits}} |- ! Michael Straczynski]] (2002–2013) | children = 1 | education = [[Carnegie Mellon University]] ([[Bachelor of Fine Arts|BFA]]) }} '''Patricia J. Tallman''' (born September 4, 1957) is an American [[actress]], [[stunt performer]], and [[studio executive]] best known for her roles in ''[[Night of the Living Dead (1990 film)|Night of the Living Dead]]'', ''[[Star Trek]]'' and ''[[Babylon 5]]''. == Early life and education == Patricia Tallman is the daughter of Jerry Tallman, a radio entertainer.{{Cite web|title=Patricia Tallman Biography (1957-)|url=http://www.filmreference.com/film/2/Patricia-Tallman.html|access-date=2012-10-10|website=www.filmreference.com}} After graduating from [[Glenbard West High School]] in [[Glen Ellyn, Illinois]] in 1975,{{Cite web|title=1975 Glenbard West High School|url=https://www.classmates.com/yearbooks/Glenbard-West-High-School/63247?page=150|access-date=2014-08-27|website=[[classmates.com]]}} she joined the theater arts program of [[Carnegie Mellon University]], which awarded her a [[Bachelor of Fine Arts]] degree.{{Cite book|last=Tallman|first=Patricia|title=Pleasure Thresholds|publisher=Publishing 180|year=2011|isbn=978-0-9821005-2-3}}{{Rp|19}}{{Cite news|last1=Arar|first1=Yardena|date=1990-10-24|title=Tallman Tumbles into Big-Time Role – 'Living Dead' Actress Dislikes Horror Pictures|page=L21|work=[[Los Angeles Daily News]]|url=https://infoweb.newsbank.com/apps/news/document-view?p=NewsBank&docref=news/0EF60E7DDF4EEC47&f=basic|access-date=2018-07-20}} == Career == In television, Tallman worked on the soap opera ''[[Generations (U.S. TV series)|Generations]]''. Later, she had guest-starring roles on ''[[Tales from the Darkside]]'', as well as the science-fiction shows ''[[Star Trek: The Next Generation]]'', ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'', and ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]''. As an actress and stunt performer, she worked on 50 episodes across the ''Star Trek'' franchise. Tallman played [[Lyta Alexander]] in the ''Babylon 5'' series pilot, recurring in seasons two and three, and starring in seasons four and five.{{Cite news|last1=Pierce|first1=Scott D.|date=1990-10-25|title='Babylon 5' full of surprises|page=S3|work=[[Deseret News]]|url=https://infoweb.newsbank.com/apps/news/document-view?p=NewsBank&docref=news/0F364C8890C6697A&f=basic|access-date=2018-07-20}} Tallman collaborated with fellow Carnegie Mellon alumnus [[George A. Romero]] on several films, including ''[[Knightriders]]'', ''[[Monkey Shines (film)|Monkey Shines]]'', and ''[[Creepshow 2]]'' (in which Tallman performed stunts).{{Cite web|last=Mennenga|first=Michael R.|date=2005-07-28|title=Slice of SciFi #17: Interview with Patricia Tallman|url=http://www.sliceofscifi.com/2005/07/28/slice-of-sci-fi-017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927190834/http://www.sliceofscifi.com/2005/07/28/slice-of-sci-fi-017|archive-date=2007-09-27|access-date=2012-10-10|website=www.sliceofscifi.com}} In 1990, Tallman starred as Barbara in the [[Tom Savini]]-directed [[Night of the Living Dead (1990 film)|remake]] of the 1968 film ''[[Night of the Living Dead]]''.{{Cite web|date=2009-10-21|title=TRINITY OF TERRORS Updates & More!|url=http://www.fangoria.com/eventsmain/weekend-of-horrors/woh-updates/118-las-vegas-2009/4350-trinity-of-terrors-updates-a-more.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091021083314/http://www.fangoria.com/eventsmain/weekend-of-horrors/woh-updates/118-las-vegas-2009/4350-trinity-of-terrors-updates-a-more.html|archive-date=2009-10-21|access-date=2021-02-21|website=[[Fangoria]]}} In 1992, she played the Possessed Witch under heavy make-up in the cult classic ''[[Army of Darkness]]'', as well as the Witch in the modern day scenes.{{citation needed|date=December 2018}} In 1993, Tallman's most notable stunt work came as stunt double for [[Laura Dern]] throughout [[Steven Spielberg]]'s ''[[Jurassic Park (film)|Jurassic Park]]''. In addition, she served as stunt double for [[Laurel Holloman]], who portrayed [[vampire hunter]] [[Justine Cooper (Angel)|Justine Cooper]] in the series ''[[Angel (1999 TV series)|Angel]]''; a photo of Tallman was also used as the photo of Justine Cooper's dead twin sister. In a 2001 episode of the TV series ''[[Sheena (TV series)|Sheena]]'', she guest-starred as the villain Caroline Dula. Tallman appeared in the 2002 psychological horror short ''Jennifer Is Dead'', the black comedy ''For Pete's Wake!'', and guest spots on ''[[Without a Trace]]'' and ''[[Castle (TV series)|Castle]]''. Tallman appeared in ''[[InAlienable]]'' (2008) and the horror film ''[[Dead Air (2009 film)|Dead Air]]'' (2009). Tallman played Holly in ''[[Atlas Shrugged: Part II]]'' (2012). Tallman has performed voice roles including playing the leading part of evil detective Jean Richmond in the Radio Repertory Company of America's production of ''Lives of the Cat'' and in some of the Anne Manx sequels (sold as radio plays on CD).{{Cite web|title=Radio Repertory Company of America|url=http://www.rrca.com/lives.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200126140509/http://www.rrca.com/lives.html|archive-date=2020-01-26|access-date=2012-02-25|website=www.rrca.com}} In 2011, Tallman published her autobiography ''Pleasure Thresholds'', the title inspired by the scene she auditioned to earn the role of Lyta Alexander. In 2012, Tallman became CEO and executive producer of [[Studio JMS]] in partnership with her then-boyfriend, [[J. Michael Straczynski]], the creator of ''[[Babylon 5]]''.{{Cite news|last=Dave|first=McNary|date=2013-02-01|title=Motion Picture Capital backs 'Flickering Light'|newspaper=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|url=https://variety.com/2013/film/news/motion-picture-capital-backs-flickering-light-1118065553/|access-date=2013-02-17}} In 2013, she left the company.{{Cite web|title=The Team|url=http://www.studiojms.com/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130603164034/http://www.studiojms.com/|archive-date=2013-06-03|access-date=2021-02-21|website=studiojms.com}} In May 2014, Tallman played the male role of Lespere in a theatrical production of Ray Bradbury's ''[[The Illustrated Man#"Kaleidoscope"|Kaleidoscope]]'' at Sci-Fest LA 2014, a theater festival.{{Cite news|last=Sutton|first=Angie Fiedler|date=2014-05-08|title=Science Fiction … Theatre?: Sci-Fest Launches With a Bang|newspaper=scifi4me.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160517090226/http://scifi4me.com/2014/05/08/science-fiction-theatre-sci-fest-launches-with-a-bang/|access-date=2014-05-10|url=http://scifi4me.com/2014/05/08/science-fiction-theatre-sci-fest-launches-with-a-bang/|archive-date=2016-05-17}} The following year Tallman played the wife in a comedy called ''[[A Logic Named Joe|A Logic Called Joe]]'' at the second Sci-Fest LA. {{Cite news|last=Boiselle|first=Matt|date=2015-05-11|title=Patricia Tallman Talks Returning to the Stage for Sci-Fest L.A.|newspaper=[[Dread Central]]|url=https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/100791/patricia-tallman-talks-working-on-the-stage-and-screen/|access-date=2015-05-13}} In 2016, Tallman started Quest Retreats, a VIP adventure excursion company with annual events in Hawaii, London, New Zealand, and South Africa.{{Cite web|title=About Pat|url=http://www.questretreats.com/about-pat/|access-date=2018-11-08|website=www.questretreats.com}} == Personal life == Tallman met Andrea Rogantini when he was the executive chef at Prego Ristorante in Los Angeles.{{Cite news|last=Perry|first=Charles|date=1993-08-08|title=THE PREGO PATTERN : Nearly 10 Years Old, This Beverly Hills Ristorante Is Still la Epitome di Una Trattoria|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1993-08-08-tm-21543-story.html|access-date=2018-11-08}} Rogantini is the father of her only child, a son named Julian Tallman.{{Rp|246}} Tallman later met Jeffrey Willerth when she was acting on ''[[Babylon 5]]'' (1993–1998), where he was an associate producer. They were married in 1999, separated several years later and divorced in 2008.{{Rp|250}} Tallman met [[J. Michael Straczynski]] (JMS) when she was acting on ''Babylon 5'', a series which he created. The two entered into a relationship some time after Straczynski separated from his wife, [[Kathryn M. Drennan]], in 2002.{{Cite web |url=https://www.facebook.com/permalink.php?story_fbid=685270231507843&id=139652459402959 |title=Hang with JMS: "Before I get into any of this... |first=J. '''Vaughn Dale Armstrong''' (born July 7, 1950) is an American actor. He is noted for portraying many characters in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise, in four [[Star Trek#Television series|''Star Trek'' television series]]. He is perhaps best known as the recurring character [[List of minor recurring characters in Star Trek: Enterprise#Maxwell Forrest|Admiral Maxwell Forrest]] in ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]''.<ref name="GuestStarProfileVaughnArmstrong">{{cite AV media |people=Vaughn Armstrong |date=April 9, 2003 |title=Guest Star Profile: Vaughn Armstrong |medium=DVD |time=7 seconds |publisher=Paramount |asin=B00062IDLA }}</ref><ref name="ign">{{cite web |date=September 14, 2001 |author=Ivan Sian |title=SciFi: Enterprise's Admiral |url=http://scifi.ign.com/articles/315160p1.html |website=[[IGN]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020209174337/http://scifi.ign.com/articles/315160p1.html |archive-date=February 9, 2002 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He has played twelve Star Trek characters.<ref>{{cite web |date=January 1, 2017 |author=Juliette Harrisson |title=Star Trek Voyager: 10 Great Guest Performances |website=[[Den of Geek]] |url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/star-trek-voyager-10-great-guest-performances/ |access-date=April 1, 2021}}</ref>

In 1985, Armstrong portrayed drill instructor Sergeant Williams in a production of the play ''Tracers'' at the Coronet Theater in Los Angeles.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mikulan |first1=Steven |title=The New 'Tracers' |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/63937280/la-weekly/ |access-date=November 24, 2020 |work=LA Weekly |date=December 5, 1985 |location=California, Los Angeles |page=72|via = [[Newspapers.com]] }}</ref> In 1989, he played Father Larkin, a priest-principal of a Catholic school, in ''Stand-up Tragedy'' at the Mark Taper Forum in Los Angeles.<ref>{{cite web |date=June 18, 1989 |first=Dan |last=Sullivan |title=An Old Story Brought Up to Speed : 'Stand-up Tragedy's' full-court press |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-06-18-ca-3770-story.html |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=An Old Story Brought Up to Speed |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/63937712/the-los-angeles-times/ |access-date=November 24, 2020 |work=The Los Angeles Times |date=June 18, 1989 |page=305|via = [[Newspapers.com]] }}</ref> In 1992 he appeared in an episode of ''[[Quantum Leap (1989 TV series)|Quantum Leap]]'' as [[Fred Trump]] (alongside his future ''Enterprise'' co-star [[Scott Bakula]]).<ref name="ign" /> In 2008, he had the role of Will Torrey, an American union representative in ''Ravensridge'' at the Fremont Centre Theatre in South Pasadena, California.<ref>{{cite news |last=Foley |first=F. Kathleen |title=Greed is native to every country |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/63938069/the-los-angeles-times/ |access-date=November 24, 2020 |newspaper=The Los Angeles Times |date=February 29, 2008 |page=72 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=February 25, 2008 |last=Mikulan |first=Steven |title=Ravensridge: Atlas Smirked |url=https://www.laweekly.com/ravensridge-atlas-smirked/ |website=[[LA Weekly]] }}</ref>
