'''Susanna Thompson''' (born January 27, 1958)<ref name=msn>{{cite web|url=http://movies.msn.com/celebrities/celebrity-biography/susanna-thompson/|title=Showtimes, reviews, trailers, news and more – MSN Movies|work=msn.com|access-date=2013-03-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111212022730/http://movies.msn.com/celebrities/celebrity-biography/susanna-thompson/|archive-date=2011-12-12|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.filmreference.com/film/68/Susanna-Thompson.html|title=Susanna Thompson Biography (1958–) |work=Film Reference |access-date=2012-06-29}}</ref> is an American actress. She is known for her roles in films ''[[Little Giants]]'' (1994), ''[[Ghosts of Mississippi]]'' (1996), ''[[Random Hearts]]'' (1999) and ''[[Dragonfly (2002 film)|Dragonfly]]'' (2002). On television, she played Dr. Lenara Kahn in the episode "[[Rejoined]]" in ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' (1995), the [[Borg]] Queen in three episodes of ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'' (1999–2000), Karen Sammler on the drama series ''[[Once and Again]]'' (1999–2002), and [[Moira Queen (Arrowverse)|Moira Queen]] on the series ''[[Arrow (TV series)|Arrow]]'' (2012–2020).

== Career ==
Thompson has appeared on stage, winning  a Dramatic Award for her role as Luisa in ''A Shayna Maidel''. She was also nominated for Best Actress by the San Diego Critics Circle for her role in ''Agnes of God''.

She may be best known for her television work, which includes playing Karen Sammler on ''[[Once and Again]]'', Michelle Generoo in [[Space (The X-Files)|an episode of ''The X-Files'']] and a recurring role as the [[Borg#Borg Queen|Borg Queen]] in the ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'' two-part episodes "[[Dark Frontier]]" (1999) and "[[Unimatrix Zero]]" (2000).<ref name=tvg /> She also portrayed Denise Hydecker in the 1998 [[television film]] ''[[The Lake (1998 film)|The Lake]]''.

One of Thompson's most controversial television appearances was on an episode of ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' titled "[[Rejoined]]". In the episode, she participated in one of US television's earlier<!-- first was 4 years earlier: "LA Law:He's a crowd"--> same-sex kisses.  The episode first aired on October 30, 1995.

She made a guest appearance on ''[[Law & Order: Special Victims Unit]]'' on October 7, 2003 in the season five episode "Mother", as Dr. Greta Heints, a [[psychiatrist]] who rehabilitates [[sex offenders]] to prepare them to return to society.

Beginning in January 2006, she had a starring role in the short-lived [[NBC]] drama ''[[The Book of Daniel (television)|The Book of Daniel]]''.<ref name=msn /> In November 2006, she made her first appearance as Army [[Lieutenant colonel (United States)|Lieutenant Colonel]] [[Hollis Mann]] on the [[CBS]] series ''[[NCIS (TV series)|NCIS]]'', in the recurring role of [[Special Agent Leroy Jethro Gibbs|Agent Gibbs]]' love interest. That same week, she appeared on ''[[Without a Trace]]''.

In 2009, Thompson starred on the short-lived NBC series ''[[Kings (American TV series)|Kings]]'', based on the biblical story of [[David]], as Queen Rose Benjamin, an analogue of [[Ahinoam]], the wife of [[Saul]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Kings |url=http://www.nbc.com/Kings/about/index.shtml# |author=NBC staff |website=[[NBC]].com |access-date=2019-01-29 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090318133805/http://www.nbc.com/Kings/about/index.shtml |archive-date=2009-03-18}}</ref>

In 2012, Thompson started a two season run as [[Moira Queen (Arrowverse)|Moira Queen]] in the main cast of the [[The CW Television Network|CW]] series ''[[Arrow (TV series)|Arrow]]'',<ref>{{cite magazine |url=http://insidetv.ew.com/2014/04/23/arrow-postmortem-moira-dead/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140424061041/http://insidetv.ew.com/2014/04/23/arrow-postmortem-moira-dead/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 24, 2014 |title='Arrow' post mortem: Boss opens up about the shocking [spoiler]! |first=Sandra |last=Gonzalez |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |date=2014-04-23 |access-date=2019-01-29}}</ref> returning as a guest in later seasons. She appeared in the recurring role of Carolyn Preston in the NBC series ''[[Timeless (American TV series)|Timeless]]'' (2016–2018).

== Personal life ==
Thompson earned her [[bachelor's degree]] in drama from [[San Diego State University]].<ref name=tvg>{{cite journal|url=https://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/susanna-thompson/bio/175829|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080530053539/http://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/susanna-thompson/bio/175829|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 30, 2008|title=Susanna Thompson|journal=[[TV Guide]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.buddytv.com/info/susanna-thompson-info.aspx|title=Susanna Thompson|website=BuddyTV.com|access-date=2012-06-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006091204/http://www.buddytv.com/info/susanna-thompson-info.aspx|archive-date=2014-10-06|url-status=dead}}</ref> Her husband, Martin B. Katz, is a professor there.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.sdjewishworld.com/2013/04/20/director-probes-the-lighter-side-of-death/ |title=Director probes the lighter side of death |last=Harrison |first=Donald H. |date=2013-04-20 |access-date=2019-01-29 |website=[[San Diego Jewish World]]}}</ref>

'''Thomas Randell Oglesby''' (born 1949) is an American actor, best known for his recurring role as [[Degra]] on ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]''. He is also known for his other ''Star Trek'' roles, including captain Trena'L in the ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'' episode "[[Unexpected (Star Trek: Enterprise)|Unexpected]]", the Miradorn twins, Ah-Kel and Ro-Kel, in the ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' episode "[[Vortex (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Vortex]]", Silaran Prin in "[[The Darkness and the Light (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|The Darkness and the Light]]" and as the telepathic alien Kir in "[[Counterpoint (Star Trek: Voyager)|Counterpoint]]", a season 5 episode of ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]''.

==Career==
Oglesby played Professor Seidel in the ''[[Angel (1999 TV series)|Angel]]'' episode "[[Supersymmetry (Angel)|Supersymmetry]]".

On ''[[Star Trek: The Next Generation]]'', Season 2 Episode 5, "[[Loud as a Whisper]]", aired January 9, 1989, he played one of three Interpreters known as Riva's Chorus.

Oglesby appeared in ''[[Independence Day (1996 film)|Independence Day]]'' (1996) as Mike Dodge. His most memorable moment is asking [[Randy Quaid]] if the aliens, who he claimed abducted him, did any "sexual things".

In 2000, he made a guest appearance as Reverend Mackee in the seventh season episode "Signs and Wonders" of ''[[The X-Files]]'', and as Joshua Vinten (the manager of formalwear rental shop) on the second last episode of TV series ''[[Columbo (TV series)|Columbo]]'' (''[[List of Columbo episodes#Season 10 and special episodes|Murder With Too Many Notes]]'').

Oglesby made a guest appearance on the ABC soap opera, ''[[General Hospital]]'' in the role of Huell on July 17, 2007. In the same year he played [[Bethlehem Steel]] executive Walter Veith in the ''[[Mad Men]]'' episode "[[New Amsterdam (Mad Men)|New Amsterdam]]".

He played Tom Jeter's father in ''[[Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip]]''.

In 2011, Oglesby played the role of Capt. Lachlan McKelty in the video game ''[[L.A. Noire]]'', that was developed by [[Team Bondi]] and [[Rockstar Games]].

In 2017, Oglesby played the role of Asa Leopold in the [[Netflix]] [[Limited series (comics)|limited series]] ''[[Godless (TV series)|Godless]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Petski |first=Denise |url=https://deadline.com/2016/09/godless-sam-waterston-kim-coates-cast-jeff-daniels-scoot-mcnairy-1201813565/|title='Godless' Adds Sam Waterston, Kim Coates, More; Scoot McNairy Confirmed|publisher=Deadline|date=September 6, 2016|accessdate=September 6, 2016}}</ref>

In 2021, he appeared as Dr. Stan Nielson in episode 3 of the [[Marvel Studios]] television miniseries ''[[WandaVision]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Hood |first=Cooper |url=https://screenrant.com/wandavision-episode-3-cast-marvel-character-guide/|title=WandaVision Episode 3 Cast Guide |publisher=ScreenRant |date=January 22, 2021 |accessdate=January 22, 2021}}</ref>

'''Marc Alaimo''' is an American actor known for his villainous roles. He is best known for his role as recurring villain [[Gul Dukat]] in the TV series ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]''.

==Early and personal life==
Alaimo grew up in [[Milwaukee, Wisconsin]]. He has a son from his first marriage, Michael Antony Alaimo, who is a [[screenwriter|writer]], [[story editor]] and [[Television producer|producer]] known for ''[[The Closer]]'', ''[[Major Crimes (TV series)|Major Crimes]]'', ''[[Invasion (2005 TV series)|Invasion]],'' ''[[Traveler (2007 TV series)|Traveler]],'' and for penning "Columbo Likes the Nightlife," the final episode of ''[[Columbo]]''.<ref>{{cite news |last=Giraud |first=Victoria |title=Area actor finds breakout role in makeup on 'Star Trek' show |department=People and Places |via=[[The Free Dictionary#The Free Library|The_Free_Library]] |url=http://www.thefreelibrary.com/AREA%2BACTOR%2BFINDS%2BBREAKOUT%2BROLE%2BIN%2BMAKEUP%2BON%2B%60STAR%2BTREK%27%2BSHOW.-a084035950 |access-date=January 15, 2025 |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Daily News]] |date=December 17, 1996 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140109092020/http://www.thefreelibrary.com/AREA+ACTOR+FINDS+BREAKOUT+ROLE+IN+MAKEUP+ON+%60STAR+TREK%27+SHOW.-a084035950 |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 9, 2014}}</ref>

==Career==
Alaimo is a classically trained theatre actor, and performed as part of the Marquette University Players and the Milwaukee Repertory Theater in the 1960s in everything from Shakespeare and the classics to world premiere productions. He was also a member of various theatre companies in New York and touring companies across the country before making the move to Los Angeles in 1973. Some of his theatrical roles include [[Iago]] in ''[[Othello]]'', Rodolpho in [[Arthur Miller]]'s ''[[A View From the Bridge]]'' and Lucky in [[Samuel Beckett]]'s ''[[Waiting for Godot]]''.

Alaimo has been playing characters in television shows since 1971. He has appeared, mostly as villains, in shows such as ''[[The Doctors (1963 TV series)|The Doctors]]'', ''[[Kojak]]'', ''[[Gunsmoke]]'', ''[[Baretta]]'', ''[[The Six Million Dollar Man]]'', ''[[The Bionic Woman]]'', ''[[Starsky & Hutch]]'', ''[[Knight Rider (1982 TV series)|Knight Rider]]'', ''[[Quincy, M.E.|Quincy]]'', ''[[The Greatest American Hero]]'', ''[[The Incredible Hulk (1978 TV series)|The Incredible Hulk]]'', ''[[Quantum Leap (1989 TV series)|Quantum Leap]]'', ''[[Family Guy]]'', ''[[Walker, Texas Ranger]]'', ''[[Wonder Woman (TV series)|Wonder Woman]]'', ''[[The Rockford Files]]'', ''[[Hill Street Blues]]'', ''[[Barnaby Jones]]'', and ''[[The A-Team]]''. Alaimo has appeared in some feature films including the 1984 science fiction movie ''[[The Last Starfighter]]'' (portraying the human guise of an alien assassin), ''[[Naked Gun 33 1/3: The Final Insult|Naked Gun {{frac|33|1|3}}: The Final Insult]]'', ''[[Tango & Cash]]'', and the 1988 film ''[[The Dead Pool]]''. He also appeared as Curtis Block in the television movie [[Case Closed (film)|''Case Closed'']] and as a security officer on Mars in the [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] movie ''[[Total Recall (1990 film)|Total Recall]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Marc Alaimo  |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/celebrity/marc_alaimo |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media]] |access-date=June 25, 2021}}</ref>

He played several characters in ''[[Star Trek: The Next Generation]]'' (''Star Trek: TNG''), starting in the first season. He has the distinction of two firsts on ''Star Trek: TNG'', playing the first [[Romulan]], Commander Tebok, in the 1988 episode "[[The Neutral Zone (Star Trek: The Next Generation)|The Neutral Zone]]", and the first [[Cardassian]] (in any ''[[Star Trek]]'' series), Gul Macet, in the 1991 episode, "[[The Wounded (Star Trek: The Next Generation)|The Wounded]]". He also played a poker player who speaks French to [[Data (Star Trek)|Data]] in the episode "[[Time's Arrow (Star Trek: The Next Generation)|Time's Arrow]]".  In 1993, Alaimo began playing Cardassian character [[Dukat (Star Trek)|Gul Dukat]] in ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]''. Gul Dukat was a recurring character that appeared in 35 episodes of the series.

Alaimo also appeared in a season two episode of ''[[21 Jump Street]]''. He was also featured in the 2006 video game ''[[Call of Juarez]]'', and its 2009 prequel ''[[Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood]]'', both times as the voice of the gunslinging Ray McCall. In 2010 he voiced The Dean in the ''[[Family Guy]]'' episode "[[The Splendid Source]]".

During a Q&A panel at the Star Trek Las Vegas Convention in 2015, Alaimo revealed he was still willing to work as an actor but was out of touch with the industry and had no agency representing him at that time.<ref>{{cite AV media |title=Andrew Robinson Alexander Siddig and Marc Alaimo Las Vegas 2015 |publisher=Knasinski, Mary|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cQz0ObRH-NQ 
|date=August 12, 2015 |access-date= April 29, 2026 |via=[[YouTube]]}}</ref>

{{short description|American actor}} {{BLP sources|date=December 2014}} {{Infobox person | name = Sherman Howard | image = Mr. Sherman Howard.jpg | alt = | caption = Howard in 2014 | birth_name = | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1949|6|11}} | birth_place = [[Chicago, Illinois]], U.S. | education = [[American Conservatory Theater]] (1971) | occupation = Actor | years_active = 1971–present | spouse = {{marriage|[[Donna Bullock (actress)|Donna Bullock]]|1988}} | children = 1 }} '''Sherman Howard''' (born June 11, 1949) is an American actor. He is best known for his performance as the zombie Bub in [[George A. Romero]]'s ''[[Day of the Dead (1985 film)|Day of the Dead]]'' (1985) and [[Lex Luthor]] on ''[[Superboy (TV series)|Superboy]]'' (1990–1992). He also voiced [[Derek Powers]] / Blight in ''[[Batman Beyond]]'' (1999–2001). ==Theatre== Howard began his career at the [[American Conservatory Theater]] (ACT) in [[San Francisco]] in 1971. While a member of ACT's repertory company, he appeared in the roles of Glendenning in [[David Storey]]'s ''The Contractor'', the archangel [[Gabriel]] in Nagle Jackson's ''The Mystery Cycle'', James in [[Harold Pinter]]'s ''[[The Collection (play)|The Collection]]'', and Gratiano in ''[[The Merchant of Venice]]'', along with roles in both ''[[Antony and Cleopatra]]'' and ''[[Caesar and Cleopatra (play)|Caesar and Cleopatra]]''. He appeared as Archie in [[Tom Stoppard]]'s ''[[Jumpers (play)|Jumpers]]'' in the premiere season of Chicago's Northlight Theatre Company. While a member of the resident company at the [[Actors Theatre of Louisville]] for three seasons during the mid-70s, he played the role of Lucius in [[Jon Jory]]'s ''Andronicus: A Space Musical'', and had roles in ''[[The Runner Stumbles]]'', ''[[The Front Page]]'', ''[[The Resistible Rise of Arturo Ui]]'', and the European tour of [[Marsha Norman]]'s ''[[Getting Out]]''. His [[off-Broadway]] credits include [[Shel Silverstein]]'s ''The Crate'' and ''The Lady or the Tiger Show'' as well as [[Sam Shepard]]'s ''[[Geography of a Horse Dreamer]]'' at the [[Ensemble Studio Theatre]], along with ''[[I'm Not Rappaport]]'' at the [[Roundabout Theatre Company]]. He appeared in ''[[Titus Andronicus]]'' and ''Tell Out My Soul'' at [[The Public Theater]], and in [[Lillian Hellman]]'s ''[[Another Part of the Forest]]'' at the Pecadillo Theatre. He most recently appeared in the title role of "Bauer" by Lauren Gunderson at 59 E 59th St in New York City. His regional credits include [[Prospero]] in ''[[The Tempest]]'', [[Henry II of England|King Henry]] in ''[[The Lion in Winter]]'', Spooner in ''[[No Man's Land (play)|No Man's Land]]'', and Lopakhin in ''[[The Cherry Orchard]]'' at the [[Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey]] (STNJ), where he has also appeared in the title roles of both [[Bertolt Brecht]]'s ''[[Life of Galileo]]'' and [[Luigi Pirandello]]'s ''[[Henry IV (Pirandello)|Henry IV]]'' (Enrico IV). He also appeared as Scrooge in the STNJ's production of ''[[A Christmas Carol]]''. He played the role of Benedick in ''[[Much Ado About Nothing]]'', opposite his wife, Donna Bullock, as Beatrice. He played the title roles in both ''[[Hamlet]]'' and ''[[Macbeth]]'' at the [[Kentucky Shakespeare Festival]] and the North Carolina Shakespeare Festival, respectively. He appeared in the title role of ''Sheridan'' at the [[La Jolla Playhouse]]. He appeared in ''[[The Price (play)|The Price]]'' at the [[Pittsburgh Public Theater]] and in ''Nine Armenians'' at the Intiman Theater in [[Seattle]]. His [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] credits include ''[[Bengal Tiger at the Baghdad Zoo]]'', ''[[All My Sons]]'', ''[[Inherit the Wind (play)|Inherit the Wind]]'', and [[Gore Vidal]]'s ''[[The Best Man (play)|The Best Man]]''. He recently concluded a run at the [[Old Globe Theatre]] in [[San Diego]] as The Player in Tom Stoppard's ''[[Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead]]'' and appeared in "The Second Mrs. Wilson" at [[George Street Playhouse]] under the direction of Gordon Edelstein. Howard also has a passion for concert hall music. In their 2013/14 season, he performed with the Philadelphia Orchestra in [[Sergei Rachmaninoff]]'s ''[[The Bells (symphony)|The Bells]]'' conducted by [[Vladimir Jurowski]]. He also appeared in the role of Prospero in the New Jersey Symphony Orchestra's presentation of [[Jean Sibelius]]' ''[[The Tempest (Sibelius)|The Tempest Suite]]'' conducted by Jacque Lacombe. He has performed [[Richard Strauss]]'s ''[[Enoch Arden (Strauss)|Enoch Arden]]'' with concert pianist David Kaplan at Bargemusic in Brooklyn and Metropolis Ensemble in Manhattan. ==Personal life== Howard has been married to actress [[Donna Bullock (actress)|Donna Bullock]] since May 1988. '''Roy Brocksmith''' (September 15, 1945 – December 16, 2001) was an American actor.

==Life and career==
Brocksmith was born in [[Quincy, Illinois]], the son of Vera Marguerite (''[[Maiden and married names|née]]'' Hartwig) and Otis E. Brocksmith, who was a [[mechanic]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Roy Brocksmith Biography (1945-) |url=http://www.filmreference.com/film/76/Roy-Brocksmith.html |website=Filmreference.com |access-date=April 15, 2025}}</ref> He graduated from [[Quincy University]] in 1970. He then moved to [[New York City]] where he began a career on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]]. His roles included Louis XIII in ''[[The Three Musketeers (musical)|The Three Musketeers]]'' and the balladeer in a revival of ''[[The Threepenny Opera]]'' with [[Raul Julia]].

Brocksmith's film and television roles included Dr. Edgemar in ''[[Total Recall (1990 film)|Total Recall]]'', a police sergeant possessed by Bill in ''[[Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey]]'', principal Michael Oslo in ''[[Picket Fences]]'' and mortician Irv Kendall in ''[[Arachnophobia (film)|Arachnophobia]]''.

He died in 2001, aged 56, from complications of [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetes]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://playbill.com/article/roy-brocksmith-actor-director-and-theatre-founder-is-dead-at-56-com-100360 |title=Roy Brocksmith, Actor, Director and Theatre Founder, Is Dead at 56 |last=Simonson |first=Robert |work=Playbill |date=December 17, 2001 |access-date=April 15, 2025}}</ref>

'''Leland Jones Orser''' (born August 6, 1960) is an American actor, director and writer. He has appeared in numerous film and television roles since his debut in 1991, notably as Lucien Dubenko on the television series ''[[ER (TV series)|ER]]'' (2004–09), Father Romero on ''[[Ray Donovan]]'' (2015–16), Richard Stratton on ''[[American Gigolo (TV series)|American Gigolo]]'' (2022), and Sam Gilroy in the ''[[Taken (franchise)|Taken]]'' film series (2008–14).

==Early life==
Orser was born in San Francisco, California  on August 6, 1960.<ref>{{cite web |title=Orser, Leland 1960– |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/education/news-wires-white-papers-and-books/orser-leland-1960 |website=[[Encyclopedia.com]] |publisher=[[Cengage]] |access-date=April 17, 2022}}</ref> He graduated from [[Connecticut College]] in 1982, and studied Acting at [[Drama Studio London]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://dramastudiolondon.co.uk/alumni/career-prospects |title=Archived copy |access-date=2019-08-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171008080431/http://www.dramastudiolondon.co.uk/alumni/career-prospects |archive-date=2017-10-08 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Rules |first1=L. |title=Famous Drama Studio London Alumni |url=https://www.ranker.com/list/famous-drama-studio-london-alumni-and-students/reference |publisher=Ranker |access-date=24 August 2019}}</ref>

==Career==
Orser began his career as a stage actor, and was nominated for a [[Helen Hayes Award|Helen Hayes Award for Best Supporting Actor]] for his performance in [[The Secret Rapture (play)|''The Secret Rapture'']] in 1991.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rose |first=Lloyd |date=18 March 1991 |title=STUDIO AMONG TOP HAYES NOMINEES |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1991/03/19/studio-among-top-hayes-nominees/c559d5cd-6d8e-4cb3-9403-3fe1f00d8619/ |work=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Nominees & Recipients Database |url=https://theatrewashington.org/helenhayesawards/nominees-recipients?tw_search=&sort_by=field_year_award_category_value&year=&theater=Olney%20Theatre%20Center&page=3 |access-date=2024-09-01 |website=TheatreWashington |language=en}}</ref> That same year, he made his television debut in 1991 on the series ''[[Gabriel's Fire]],'' and went on to appear in programs such as ''[[The Golden Girls]]'', ''[[Cheers]]'', ''[[L.A. Law]]'', ''[[The X-Files]]'', ''[[NYPD Blue]]'', ''[[The Pretender (TV series)|The Pretender]]'', ''[[Law & Order: Special Victims Unit]]'' and ''[[CSI: Crime Scene Investigation]]''. In 1999, he played Dr. Arthur Zeller in ''[[The Outer Limits (1995 TV series)|The Outer Limits]]'' episode "[[Descent (The Outer Limits)|Descent]]".

He appeared in ''[[Seven (1995 film)|Seven]]'' (1995) as a man who was involuntarily recruited to kill a prostitute. He was credited as "Crazed Man in Massage Parlour". He played Larry Purvis in ''[[Alien Resurrection]]'' (1997).

He played the antagonist Richard Thompson in the [[Denzel Washington]] thriller ''[[The Bone Collector]]'' (1999). In 2001, he had a role in ''[[Pearl Harbor (film)|Pearl Harbor]]'' as an injured officer saved by [[Kate Beckinsale]]'s character. In 2003, he appeared as [[James Wesley (comics)|Wesley Owen Welch]] in the [[Marvel Comics]] superhero film ''[[Daredevil (film)|Daredevil]]''. 

Orser also appeared in various roles in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise, among them playing a [[Changelings (Star Trek)|Changeling]] posing as the [[Romulan]] [[Colonel]] Lovok in the ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' episode "[[The Die Is Cast (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|The Die Is Cast]]" and in the episode "[[Sanctuary (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Sanctuary]]" playing a bit part as a member of the Skrreean race. He also played a homicidal [[hologram]] in the ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'' episode "[[Revulsion (Star Trek: Voyager)|Revulsion]]". In ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'', he played the character "Loomis" in the time-travel episode "[[Carpenter Street (Star Trek: Enterprise)|Carpenter Street]]".<ref>[http://www.littlereview.com/getcritical/trektalk/orser.htm "The Alien Resurrection of Leland Orser"], littlereview.com; retrieved February 10, 2006.</ref>

He played Ansel in the drama thriller film ''[[Faults (film)|Faults]]''.<ref>[http://www.dreadcentral.com/news/92234/today-vod-find-faults ''Faults'' (film)], dreadcentral.com; accessed November 7, 2016.</ref> From 2004–09, he played Chief of Surgery Dr. Lucien Dubenko, a recurring character, on ''[[ER (TV series)|ER]]''. Most recently he has appeared as Sam in all three of the [[Taken (film series)|''Taken'' film series]].

In 2010, Orser made his directorial debut with the film ''[[Morning (film)|Morning]].''

==Personal life==
Orser married [[Roma Downey]] in 1987; they divorced in 1989. In 2000, he married [[Jeanne Tripplehorn]], with whom he had co-starred in [[Peter Berg]]'s dark comedy ''[[Very Bad Things]]''; they have one son.<ref name=sfgate>{{cite web|url=http://www.sfgate.com/entertainment/article/S-F-native-Orser-opens-dark-door-as-director-3266701.php|title=S. F. native Orser opens dark door as director|date=April 24, 2010|author=Peter Hartlaub|work=San Francisco Chronicle|access-date=February 18, 2013}}</ref>

'''Gregory Martin Itzin'''<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gregorymartinitzin.com/ |title=Gregory Itzin Official Website |website=Gregorymartinitzin.com |access-date=August 27, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130612131840/http://www.gregorymartinitzin.com/ |archive-date=June 12, 2013}}</ref> (April 20, 1948 – July 8, 2022) was an American character actor of film and television best known for his role as [[President of the United States|U.S. President]] [[Charles Logan (24)|Charles Logan]] in the action thriller series ''[[24 (TV series)|24]]''.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Nolfi |first1=Joey |title=Gregory Itzin, '24' and 'Star Trek' actor, dies at 74 |url=https://ew.com/celebrity/gregory-itzin-dead-24-actor-dies-at-74/ |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |date=July 8, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Evans |first1=Greg |date=July 8, 2022 |title=Gregory Itzin Dies: Actor Who Played '24' President Charles Logan Was 74 |url=https://deadline.com/2022/07/gregory-itzin-dead-obituary-24-actor-was-74-1235060294/ |access-date=July 8, 2022 |work=[[Deadline Hollywood]]}}</ref>

==Early life==
Itzin was born in Washington, D.C., the son of Evelyn Loretta (née Smith) and Martin Joseph Itzin.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.itzin.com/Roots/Webfiles/Conrad_Brenneisen/b188.htm |title=Fourteenth Generation |website=Itzin.com |access-date=August 27, 2013}}</ref> When he was in sixth grade, his family moved to [[Burlington, Wisconsin]], where his father was mayor. Itzin originally intended to become a theater actor, receiving training at the [[American Conservatory Theater]] in San Francisco. He acted on many stages across the country.

==Career==

=== Television ===
Itzin first appeared on television as a contestant on ''[[Whew!]]'' in 1979, then in guest starring roles on various television shows like in the ''[[MacGyver (1985 TV series)|MacGyver]]'' episode "Final Approach" (1986). He received a [[Tony Award]] nomination for his role in the Pulitzer Prize–winning play ''[[The Kentucky Cycle]]''. In the movie ''[[Airplane!]]'', Itzin played Religious Zealot #1. He had a small role in ''[[The A-Team]]'' episode "Wheel of Fortune" as Howard, an accountant at a casino.

In 2005, Itzin joined the cast of ''[[24 (TV series)|24]]'', halfway through its fourth season, in the recurring role as Vice President [[Charles Logan (24 character)|Charles Logan]]. By the following season the character had become President and was expanded to become one of the leading figures in the storyline. Itzin received an [[Emmy Award|Emmy]] nomination for [[Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series|Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series]] for this performance. He didn't have to audition for the role, since he had previously auditioned for a role during the second season of the show, and knew one of the producers.<ref>{{cite magazine |first=Jenelle |last=Riley |url=http://www.backstage.com/bso/news_reviews/features/feature_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1003122499 |title=Head of the (White) House |date=September 14, 2006 |magazine=[[Backstage (magazine)|Backstage]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070313055258/http://www.backstage.com/bso/news_reviews/features/feature_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1003122499 |archive-date=March 13, 2007}}</ref> Itzin returned for four episodes in [[24 (season 6)|season six]]. Itzin returned for a story arc during the [[24 (season 8)|eighth season]] of the show to help [[Allison Taylor|President Allison Taylor]] keep the Peace Treaty alive.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Ausiello |first=Michael |author-link=Michael Ausiello |url=https://ew.com/article/2009/11/01/24-scoop-president-logan-returns/ |title='24' scoop: President Logan returns! |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |date=November 1, 2009 |access-date=August 27, 2013 |archive-date=June 9, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150609004838/http://www.ew.com/article/2009/11/01/24-scoop-president-logan-returns |url-status=dead }}</ref> This resulted in an Emmy nomination for [[Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series#2010s|Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.emmys.com/sites/emmys.com/files/62ndemmys_noms.pdf |title=Emmy nomination list |page=21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110227010617/http://www.emmys.com/sites/emmys.com/files/62ndemmys_noms.pdf |archive-date=February 27, 2011}}</ref> Somewhat coincidentally, before this role, Itzin played a Presidential Candidate in a commercial for cheese products, who was deemed a "doofus" for not liking cheese.

In 2007, he made a guest appearance as William Adama, Dick Tracy, and a police officer at Randy's Halloween night in an episode of ''[[Robot Chicken]]''.

Itzin has held recurring roles on popular TV series such as ''[[Friends]]'' as [[List of Friends and Joey characters#Theodore and Bitsy Hannigan|Theodore Hannigan]], father of [[Mike Hannigan]], ''[[Murder One (TV series)|Murder One]]'', ''[[NCIS (TV series)|NCIS]]'', and ''[[The Mentalist]]''. He played [[Virgil Minelli|the head of the unit]] in the latter for 13 episodes, before leaving to return to ''24'' for its final season. Itzin also appeared on ''[[Night Court]]'', ''[[Matlock (1986 TV series)|Matlock]]'', ''[[Diagnosis: Murder]]'', ''[[Jake and the Fatman]]'', ''[[The O.C.]]'', ''[[Beverly Hills, 90210]]'', ''[[Judging Amy]]'', ''[[Boston Legal]]'', ''[[CSI: Crime Scene Investigation]]'', ''[[The Practice]]'', ''[[The Pretender (TV series)|The Pretender]]'' and the short-lived science fiction series, ''[[Firefly (TV series)|Firefly]]''. He also portrayed [[John Ashcroft]] in the 2003 television movie ''[[DC 9/11: Time of Crisis]]''. He had a recurring role on ''[[Covert Affairs]]''.

Itzin made his first ''Star Trek'' appearance in 1993, in the ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' episode "[[Dax (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine episode)|Dax]]". He became a frequent ''[[Star Trek]]'' actor, playing five different roles in the various series over the years, and guest starred on ''DS9'' again in the sixth-season episode "[[Who Mourns for Morn?]]". He appeared as Doctor Dysek in the episode "[[Critical Care (Star Trek: Voyager)|Critical Care]]" in the 7th season of ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]''. His most recent ''Trek'' role was [[Admiral Black (Star Trek)|Admiral Black]] in ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]''.

Itzin was a special guest star on the Disney Channel hit show ''[[Hannah Montana]]'' in the season two episode "Test of My Love" as a billionaire whose son becomes a romantic interest of Miley's. He hosted ''ACME: This Week!'' at the [[ACME Comedy Theatre]] on February 23, 2008, appearing in several sketches as well as a short film, "Law and Order: Really Special Victims Unit". Itzin  had a recurring role in seasons 1–4 of USA Network's series, ''[[Covert Affairs]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Abrams |first1=Natalie |title=24's Gregory Itzin Heading to Covert Affairs |url=https://www.tvguide.com/news/24s-gregory-itzin-1019051/ |website=[[TV Guide]] |access-date=July 12, 2022|date=May 28, 2010}}</ref>

=== Theater ===
On stage, he appeared in numerous theatrical venues across the country. Itzin was a member of the [[Antaeus Theatre Company]] in Los Angeles.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2010-06-26 |title=Gregory Itzin, slimy villain of '24,' plays noble good guy in Antaeus Co.'s 'King Lear' |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/blogs/culture-monster-blog/story/2010-06-26/gregory-itzin-slimy-villain-of-24-plays-noble-good-guy-in-antaeus-co-s-king-lear |access-date=2026-08-30 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref> He was also a member of the [[The Matrix Theatre Company|Matrix Theatre Company]] in Los Angeles, where he acted in award-winning productions of ''[[Waiting for Godot]]'', ''[[The Homecoming]]'', and ''[[The Birthday Party (play)|The Birthday Party]]'' (each earning him an L.A. Drama Critics Circle Award for performance). For his work in the [[Pulitzer Prize for Drama|Pulitzer Prize]]-winning ''[[The Kentucky Cycle]]'' — which he performed in the world premiere at the [[Intiman Theatre Festival|Intiman Theatre]], [[Mark Taper Forum]], the [[John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts|Kennedy Center]], and on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] — he received [[Tony Award]] and [[Drama Desk Award]] nominations.

He appeared on stage as Louis de Rougemont in the world premiere of [[Donald Margulies]]' ''Shipwrecked! An Entertainment'' at [[South Coast Repertory]], and subsequently revived at the [[Geffen Playhouse]].

In 2010, he appeared as the Earl of Kent in the Antaeus Company's production of ''King Lear.'' He won the L.A. Drama Critics Circle Award for this performance.

He was in several radio plays with The [[L.A. Theatre Works]], and played the Archbishop in the [[Hollywood Theater of the Ear]]'s 2010 audio production of ''[[Saint Joan (play)|Saint Joan]]''.

=== Film ===
Itzin starred in ''[[Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (film)|Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas]]'' as a [[The Mint Las Vegas|Mint Hotel]] clerk, who looked and sounded a lot like actor [[McLean Stevenson]] on ''[[M*A*S*H (TV series)|M*A*S*H]]''. He played a psychiatrist in the [[Lindsay Lohan]] thriller ''[[I Know Who Killed Me]]'' and as a prison warden in ''[[Law Abiding Citizen]]''. His final film role was as [[James Bond (ornithologist)]] in the 2022 British documentary ''[[The Other Fellow (2022 film)|The Other Fellow]]''.

==Personal life, health and death==
Itzin and his wife, Judie, whom he married in 1979, had two children.<ref name="Wenger">{{cite news |url=https://people.com/tv/gregory-itzin-dead/ |title=24 and NCIS Star Gregory Itzin Dead at 74 |last=Wenger |first=Stephanie |date=July 8, 2022 |access-date=July 9, 2022 |work=[[People (magazine)|People]]}}</ref>

Itzin had a "major heart attack" in 2015, but was able to continue acting.<ref name="Wenger" /> He died on July 8, 2022, at the age of 74 due to complications during an emergency surgery.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/drama/gregory-itzin-dead-24-newsupdate/|title=Gregory Itzin, 24 and Star Trek actor, dies, aged 74|work=[[Radio Times]]|first=Minnie|last=Wright|date=July 8, 2022|access-date=July 8, 2022}}</ref>

[[University of California, Los Angeles]] ([[Master of Arts|M.A.]], Theatre Arts) | occupation = Actor | years_active = 1965–2007 | spouse = {{Marriage|[[Meredith Baxter]]
|1974|1989|end=div.}} | children = 3 }} '''David Edwin Birney''' (April 23, 1939 – April 27, 2022) was an American actor and director whose career included performances in both contemporary and classical roles in theatre, film, and television. He is noted for having played the title role in the television series ''[[Serpico (TV series)|Serpico]]''. He also starred in ''[[Bridget Loves Bernie]]'', an early 1970s TV series about an interfaith marriage that also starred [[Meredith Baxter]], whom he married after the series ended. He also portrayed Dr. Ben Samuels in ''[[St. Elsewhere]]'' from 1982 until 1983. ==Early life== Birney was born to an [[Irish Catholic]] family in [[Washington, D.C.]], on April 23, 1939. His father, Edwin, worked as a special agent for the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]]; his mother, Jeanne (née McGee), was a housewife before becoming a real estate agent.{{cite news|title=David Birney, Who Starred in TV's 'Bridget Loves Bernie,' Dies at 83|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/05/02/arts/television/david-birney-dead.html|first=Richard|last=Sandomir| date=May 2, 2022| access-date=May 3, 2022| id={{Gale|A702389440}} | page=A26(L) | newspaper=[[The New York Times]]}} Birney attended schools in [[Brooklyn, Ohio]], and graduated from West High School in [[Cleveland]]. Named to the [[National Honor Society]], he lettered in basketball, football, and track. He held a [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] degree from [[Dartmouth College]] with "High Distinction" in English literature, English Honors. At the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], Birney earned an [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] in theatre arts, acting and directing, studying with Ralph Freud and William Melnitz. He held a teaching assistant fellowship and was awarded an honorary [[Ph.D.]] in Humanities from [[Southern Utah University]].{{cite web| title=Honorary Degree Recipients: 1987| url=https://www.suu.edu/trustees/honorary-degree-recipients.html| access-date=November 8, 2021| website=Southern Utah University}} ==Career== ===Stage=== While in the [[U.S. Army]], Birney won an All Army Entertainment contest and received the "[[Barter Theatre]] Award" in 1965. Since the award was an equity contract with the Company for an entire season, he consequently spent the next season with the [[Barter Theatre]], the State Theatre of Virginia, starring or appearing in fifteen shows, directing two others. In the following two years he went on to perform with a range of companies and productions, [[off-Broadway]] and in several regional repertory theatres. His New York debut was with [[Joseph Papp|Joe Papp]]'s [[New York Shakespeare Festival]] as Antipholus of Syracuse in [[William Shakespeare]]’s ''[[The Comedy of Errors]]''. Birney worked continually in the theatre performing leading roles with some of the most important theatres in the country. His stage credits included starring roles on Broadway in ''[[Amadeus (play)|Amadeus]]'', ''[[Benefactors (play)|Benefactors]]'',{{cite web|title=Actor David Birney in a scene fr. the replacement cast of the Broadway play "Benefactors." (New York)|url=https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/b4238231-57aa-56ba-e040-e00a18066127|access-date=May 3, 2022|publisher=New York Public Library}}{{cite magazine|last1=|first1=|date=June 23, 1986|title=Theater Listings: Now Playing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mucCAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA83|magazine=Billboard|publisher=New York Media, LLC|volume=19|issue=25|page=83|issn=0028-7369}} and Aside from his title role in ''Bridget Loves Bernie'', Birney appeared frequently on television, building a career in TV movies, regular series and [[miniseries]]. He starred in such series as ''[[Live Shot]]'', ''[[Cannon (TV series)|Cannon]]'', ''[[St. Elsewhere]]'', ''[[The Adams Chronicles]]'', ''[[Glitter (American TV series)|Glitter]]'',{{cite news |last1=Rothenberg |first1=Fred |title='Happy Days' Makes Way for New Shows |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1356&dat=19840502&id=XQIzAAAAIBAJ&pg=6979,680327 |access-date=April 21, 2020 |newspaper=[[Star–Banner|Ocala Star-Banner]] |date=May 2, 1984 |page=16}} ''Serpico'',{{cite news |last1=Holsapple |first1=Barbara |title=McMurray Child on 'Missing' | department=Midnight Movies|via=Google Newspapers |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1144&dat=19860115&id=MhwhAAAAIBAJ&pg=1755,6312339 |access-date=April 21, 2020 |newspaper=[[The Pittsburgh Press]] |date=January 15, 1986 |page=C11}} ''[[Fantasy Island]]'', ''[[Hawaii Five-O (1968 TV series)|Hawaii Five-O]]'', ''[[McMillan & Wife]]'', ''[[The F.B.I. (TV series)|The F.B.I.]]'', and ''[[Murder, She Wrote]]''.{{cite news |title=New Years |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1310&dat=19881231&id=nPFVAAAAIBAJ&pg=2563,8114457 |access-date=April 21, 2020 |newspaper=[[The Register-Guard]] |date=December 31, 1988 |location=Eugene, Oregon |page=24}} He also starred in the episode "The Nomads" from the 1977 series ''[[Quinn Martin's Tales of the Unexpected]]'', known in the United Kingdom as ''Twist in the Tale''.{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/tales_of_the_unexpected_1977 |title=Tales of the Unexpected|website=Rotten Tomatoes|access-date=May 3, 2022}} His miniseries credits include ''[[Testimony of Two Men]]'', ''[[Jacqueline Susann's Valley of the Dolls|Valley of the Dolls]]'', ''[[Night of the Fox]]'', and ''[[Master of the Game (novel)#Adaptations|Master of the Game]]''. He also appeared in the TV series the Love Boat with his wife where he played an Italian escort to an American woman whose friend arranged the encounter. Birney also appeared in leading roles in many television films, including ''[[The Irish in America: Long Journey Home|Long Journey Home]]'' and ''[[Serpico (TV series)|The Deadly Game]]''. He also appeared in the soap operas ''[[The Best of Everything (TV series)|The Best of Everything]]'' and ''[[Love Is a Many Splendored Thing (TV series)|Love Is a Many Splendored Thing]]''.{{cite book| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NUXIAgAAQBAJ&q=david+birney+love+is+a+many&pg=PA2121| title=Encyclopedia of Television| last=Newcomb| first=Horace| date=2014| publisher=Routledge| isbn=978-1-1351-9472-7| page=2121| via=Google Books}} ===Writing and directing=== Birney edited and adapted for the stage a two-character play based on some of [[Mark Twain]]’s shorter works and letters. The piece, ''Mark Twain's The Diaries of Adam and Eve'', was presented on the [[PBS]] series ''[[American Playhouse]]''.{{cite book| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VYsavOLN8HQC&q=david+birney+adam+eve+pbs+american+playhouse&pg=PA118| title=Critical Companion to Mark Twain: A Literary Reference to His Life and Work| last=Rasmussen| first=R. Kent| publisher=Infobase Publishing| year=2014| isbn=978-1-4381-0852-0| page=118}} Developing the play subsequently for the stage, Birney directed and starred in productions for regional theatres such as the [[Hartford Stage]] (opening the Mark Twain Festival in Hartford), the [[Capital Repertory Theatre]], and on tour in performing arts centers across the country. A second play, ''A Christmas Pudding'', a Christmas collage of song, story and poetry of the season was published by [[Samuel French, Inc.]]{{cite web| title=David Birney| url=https://www.concordtheatricals.com/a/310/david-birney| website=Concord Theatricals| access-date=November 8, 2021}} ===Professional associations=== Birney served on the Large Theatre Panel of the [[National Endowment for the Arts]] and was a board member of the [[Foundation for Biomedical Research]]. He also served on the Theatre and Dance Panel of the Jacob Javits Fellowship Foundation. For Dartmouth College he served as a member of the Board of Overseers for the [[Hopkins Center for the Arts]]. He initiated and chaired the Class of '61 Legacy: The American Tradition in Performance, helping to create a substantial endowment dedicated to live performance at the Hopkins Center at Dartmouth College.{{cite web| title=The Arts at Dartmouth Awards Ceremony| url=https://hop.dartmouth.edu/sites/hop.prod/files/hop/content/production-season/resource-file/artsawards2020playbill-final.pdf| date=May 26, 2020| website=Dartmouth College Department of Theater| access-date=November 8, 2021}} For five years, Birney co-chaired the [[American Diabetes Association]], speaking and fund raising for the Association. He was an advisor for the Children’s Rights Council, a national nonprofit organization advocating access to both parents after divorce or separation. His contribution to classical theatre was recognized with Washington's Shakespeare Theatre's Millennium Award. ==Personal life== Birney married actress [[Meredith Baxter]] in 1974. They had starred together in the 1972–73 TV series ''[[Bridget Loves Bernie]]''. During their marriage, she was known as Meredith Baxter Birney. Together, they had three children: Kate, Mollie, and Peter. They divorced in 1989. In 2011, she said Birney emotionally and physically abused her during their marriage.{{cite news| title=Meredith Baxter Alleges Ex-Husband David Birney Abused Her| url=https://abcnews.go.com/Entertainment/actress-meredith-baxter-abused-husband-david-birney/story?id=13029302| last=James| first=Susan Donaldson| date=December 2, 2009| work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]| access-date=November 8, 2021}} He published a lengthy statement on his website disputing the allegations.{{cite web| title='Untied' A Statement| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110619120632/http://davidbirney.com/UntiedStatement.pdf| archive-date=June 19, 2011| url=http://davidbirney.com/UntiedStatement.pdf| url-status=usurped| website=DavidBirney}}{{cite news| title=David Birney Denies Abuse Claims by Meredith Baxter| url=https://people.com/celebrity/david-birney-denies-abuse-claims-by-meredith-baxter/| date=March 4, 2011| first=Mike| last=Fleeman| journal=[[People (magazine)|People]]| access-date=November 8, 2021}} ==Death== In the December 2017 edition of the ''Wide Wide World'' newsletter for [[Dartmouth College]] class of 1961 alumni, it was disclosed that Birney had been diagnosed with [[Alzheimer's disease]].{{cite journal| url=http://dartmouth.imodules.com/s/1353/images/gid7/editor_documents/newsletters/2017/december/1961_december_2017.pdf| date=December 2017| page=5| title=Green Cards| last=Bloom| first=Arthur| journal=Wide Wide World| access-date=November 8, 2021}} Birney died on April 27, 2022, four days after his 83rd birthday, at his home in [[Santa Monica, California]]. At the time of his death, he was in a domestic partnership with Michele Roberge.{{cite web |url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/david-birney-dead-actor-bridget-loves-bernie-83-1235139638 |title=David Birney, Actor on 'Bridget Loves Bernie' and 'St. Elsewhere', Dies at 83 |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |author=Mike Barnes |date=May 3, 2022}} ==Filmography== ===Film=== *''[[Caravan to Vaccarès (film)|Caravan to Vaccarès]]'' (1974){{cite magazine|first=Stephen|last=Vagg|date=22 August 2025|access-date=22 August 2025|magazine=Filmink|url=https://www.filmink.com.au/forgotten-british-film-studios-the-rank-organisation-1968-1977/|title=Forgotten British Film Studios: The Rank Organisation 1968-1977}}{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/celebrity/david_birney|title=David Birney|website=Rotten Tomatoes|access-date=May 3, 2022}}{{cite web|url=https://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/person/16470%7C0/David-Birney#filmography|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160127155926/http://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/person/16470%7C0/David-Birney/#filmography|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 27, 2016|title=David Birney – Filmography|publisher=Turner Classic Movies|access-date=May 3, 2022}} – Bowman *''[[Trial by Combat]]'' (1976){{cite web|url=https://catalog.afi.com/Person/252176-David-Birney|title=David Birney|publisher=American Film Institute|access-date=May 3, 2022}}{{cite web|url=https://www2.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2ba063807c|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190307161310/http://www.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2ba063807c|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 7, 2019|title=David Birney|publisher=British Film Institute|access-date=May 3, 2022}} – Sir John Gifford *''[[Bye, See You Monday]]'' (1979){{cite web|title=David Birney List of Movies and TV Shows|url=https://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/david-birney/credits/3000527738/|website=TV Guide|access-date=May 3, 2022}} – Frank *''[[Oh, God! [[University of California, Irvine]] | occupation = Actor | years_active = 1984–present | known_for = [[Cobra (1986 film)]] | spouse = | children = 2 | website = }} '''Brian Earl Thompson''' (born August 28, 1959) is an American [[actor]]. His career began with a small role in the 1984 film ''[[The Terminator]]''. He played the villainous "Night Slasher" in the 1986 film ''[[Cobra (1986 film)|Cobra]]''. His first named role was on ''[[Werewolf (TV series)|Werewolf]]'', a horror series that ran during [[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox]]'s inaugural broadcasting year of 1987–1988.{{cite news|last1=Schneider|first1=Michael|title=Fox hunting werewolves|url=https://variety.com/2009/scene/news/fox-hunting-werewolves-1118012222|access-date=October 28, 2014|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=December 3, 2009}}{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0092480|website=IMDb|access-date=October 28, 2014|title=''Werewolf'' television series profile}} Thompson has played several characters in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise—the most notable being the Klingon Lieutenant Klag, who informed Commander [[William Riker]] that "Gagh is always best when served live", the [[Colonist (The X-Files)#Alien Bounty Hunters|Alien Bounty Hunter]] on ''[[The X-Files]]'', and Eddie Fiori on ''[[Kindred: The Embraced]]''.{{cite web|last1=SFX Staff Writer|title=SF's Serial Guest Stars|url=http://www.sfx.co.uk/2011/06/02/sf%E2%80%99s-greatest-guest-stars/|website=SFX.com|access-date=October 28, 2014|date=June 2, 2011}} In 2014, he produced, wrote and starred in the [[B movie]] [[parody]] ''[[The Extendables]]''.{{cite web|last1=Man|first1=Wild Peking|title=Brian Thompson and Mark Dacascos are 'The Extendables'|url=http://www.cityonfire.com/brian-thompson-and-mark-dacascos-are-the-extendables|website=City on Fire|access-date=October 28, 2014|date=November 23, 2013}} ==Early life== Thompson was born in [[Ellensburg, Washington]], and raised in [[Longview, Washington|Longview]]. He attended [[Central Washington University]], where he studied business management, played football, and appeared in many school productions. He then moved to California and earned a [[Master of Fine Arts]] from the [[University of California, Irvine]].{{cite web|last1=WGA|title=Brian Thompson|url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0859921|website=IMDb|access-date=October 28, 2014}} He initially trained and pursued a career in musical theater, performing at Riverside Civil Light Opera's production of ''[[The King and I]]'', Long Beach Civic Light Opera's ''[[Bitter Sweet (operetta)|Bitter Sweet]]'', and several other musicals. In 1982, he was a resident actor at the [[Colorado Shakespeare Festival]]. Thompson's athletic build and unique facial structure were key in the initial roles he was offered.{{cite web|title=The Working Class - Brian Thompson|url=http://www.culturalatrocities.com/2011/09/working-class-brian-thompson.html|website=Cultural Atrocities|access-date=October 28, 2014|date=September 19, 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141029005506/http://www.culturalatrocities.com/2011/09/working-class-brian-thompson.html|archive-date=October 29, 2014}} He has stated that it has occasionally been a double-edged sword when it comes to auditioning for roles, but it has provided him with consistent work.{{cite web|last1=Eramo|first1=Steve|title=Sci-Fi Blast From The Past - Brian Thompson (Star Trek: The Next Generation)|url=http://scifiandtvtalk.typepad.com/scifiandtvtalk/2011/03/sci-fi-blast-from-the-past-brian-thompson-star-trek-the-next-generation.html|publisher=SciFi TV & Talk|access-date=October 28, 2014|date=March 15, 2011}} Thompson said, "If you're very physical in stature, you're gonna get hired for action movies. The star's always going to be chasing someone so they need an equal adversary. I'm never going to play a nebbish geek." ==Career== Thompson was cast in ''[[The Terminator]]'' while still in school. He and [[Bill Paxton]] had minor roles as punk thugs.{{cite web|last1=Bolotin|first1=Louise|title=INTERVIEW: Action star Brian Thompson on The Terminator|url=http://www.screenjabber.com/interview-action-star-brian-thompson-terminator|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121014003641/http://www.screenjabber.com/interview-action-star-brian-thompson-terminator|url-status=usurped|archive-date=October 14, 2012|website=Screen Jabber|access-date=October 28, 2014|date=June 10, 2012}}{{cite news|last1=Nelson|first1=Craig|title=Manchester film fans turned out for a special screening of The Terminator and we interview Brian Thompson.|url=http://www.manchestergossip.com/film/05-october-2012/2760/manchester_film_fans_special_screening_terminator_interview_brian_thompson|access-date=October 28, 2014|publisher=Manchester Gossip|date=October 5, 2012|archive-date=October 29, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141029003138/http://www.manchestergossip.com/film/05-october-2012/2760/manchester_film_fans_special_screening_terminator_interview_brian_thompson|url-status=dead}} He followed that up with roles on ''[[Moonlighting (TV series)|Moonlighting]]'', ''[[Otherworld (TV series)|Otherworld]]'', ''[[Street Hawk]]'' and ''[[Knight Rider (1982 TV series)|Knight Rider]]'' before landing a role in the [[Sylvester Stallone]] vehicle, ''[[Cobra (1986 film)|Cobra]]'' (1986). Although the film was critically panned, it was a commercial success. ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote of Thompson's portrayal, "the archvillain, a character that is a cross between a [[James Bond]] fantasy villain such as [[Jaws (James Bond)|Jaws]] and a raging psychopath, delivers a scorching monologue – a feat of linguistic sophistication that Cobra would have a hard time matching."{{cite news|last1=Darnton|first1=Nina|title=FILM: SYLVESTER STALLONE AS POLICEMAN, IN 'COBRA'|url=https://www.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9A0DE5DF103AF937A15756C0A960948260|access-date=28 October 2014|work=New York Times|date=May 24, 1986}} In 1993, Thompson landed another comedic role on the large ensemble series ''[[Key West (TV series)|Key West]]'' which was filmed on location in the [[Florida Keys]]. The series lasted for 13 episodes. He played a "new-age sheriff", which Thompson has stated was the favorite role of his career. The character uttered the introductory line, "I'm Sheriff Cody Jeremiah Jefferson. I'm a direct descendant of [[Wyatt Earp]] and [[the Lone Ranger]]. My personal heroes are [[Ted Nugent]], [[Buddha]] and [[Davy Crockett]]. I am the last real lawman and the first peace officer of the 21st century."{{cite news|last1=Hiltbrand|first1=David|title=Picks and Pans Review: Key West|url=http://www.people.com/people/archive/article/0,,20109596,00.html|access-date=October 28, 2014|work=People Magazine|date=January 18, 1993}} The following year, Thompson began his tenure on ''The X-Files'' and followed that with roles in the science fiction-fantasy series ''[[Seven Days (TV series)|Seven Days]]'', ''[[Buffy the Vampire Slayer]]'' and ''[[Charmed]]''. Between these, Thompson made dozens of appearances in other series and films. In 1996, he appeared in ''[[Dragonheart]]'' as Brok, the commander of the armies of [[David Thewlis]]' villainous king, Einon. The [[fantasy film]], starring [[Dennis Quaid]] and [[Sean Connery]], was a moderate success.{{cite news|last1=Tucker|first1=Ken|title=Dragonheart (1996)|url=https://ew.com/article/1996/06/07/dragonheart/|access-date=28 October 2014|work=Entertainment Weekly (EW)|date=June 7, 1996}} Thompson then returned to the big screen as lead antagonist [[Shao Kahn]] in the poorly received ''[[Mortal Kombat Annihilation]]''.{{cite web|last1=Staff Writers|title=MORTAL KOMBAT: ANNIHILATION (1997)|url=http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/mortal_kombat_annihilation/|website=Rotten Tomatoes|access-date=October 28, 2014}} ''[[The New York Times]]'' called it "colossal compendium of logic-defying martial arts, noisy, hyperactive special effects..."{{cite news|last1=VanGelder|first1=Lawrence|title=Mortal Kombat The Annihilation (1997) FILM REVIEW; Based on a Video Game. Need to Know More?|url=https://www.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9803E2D6123BF931A15752C1A961958260|access-date=October 28, 2014|work=New York Times|date=November 22, 1997}} In 2014, Thompson released ''The Extendables'', a film he produced, wrote, and starred in. A parody of movies like ''[[The Expendables (2010 film)|The Expendables]]'', Thompson stated that it contained true-to-life instances from his own career.{{cite web|last1=Valkor|title=The Extendables Movie Review|url=http://www.the-other-view.com/the-extendables.html|website=The Other View|access-date=October 28, 2014|date=August 22, 2014}} It was released via [[iTunes]].{{cite web|last1=Staff|title=The Extendables|url=https://itunes.apple.com/us/movie/the-extendables/id902097318|website=iTunes|access-date=October 28, 2014}} In 2017 Thompson was in the thriller indie film ''[[Trafficked]]'' with [[Ashley Judd]],{{cite web | url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-reviews/trafficked-1046156/ | title='Trafficked': Film Review | website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] | date=5 October 2017 |last1=Scheck|first1=Frank}} and in 2019 he starred in the horror film ''[[Hoax (2019 film)|Hoax]]'' alongside [[Adrienne Barbeau]];{{cite web | url=https://www.joblo.com/trailer-brian-thompson-learns-bigfoot-is-not-a-hoax-this-august/ | title=Trailer: Brian Thompson learns Bigfoot is not a Hoax this August | date=29 July 2019 }} in 2022 he appeared in the historical thriller film ''[[The Tragedy of Macbeth (2021 film)|The Tragedy of Macbeth]]'' with [[Denzel Washington]]. ===''Star Trek''=== In 1989, Thompson landed his first ''Star Trek'' role on ''[[Star Trek: The Next Generation]]''. His size worked against him at first, because the producers were originally looking to cast someone who could fit in a certain costume. He was able to convince them to give him a try: "That was the first of five auditions that I've had for ''Star Trek'' and they've hired me every time." Thompson played a [[Klingon]] in the episode "[[A Matter of Honor]]".{{cite web|last1=Tenuto|first1=John|title=REVIEW: Star Trek: The Next Generation Season 2 on Blu-ray|url=http://www.treknews.net/2012/12/17/review-star-trek-tng-season-2-blu-ray|website=Trek News.Com|access-date=October 28, 2014|date=December 17, 2012}} In 1993 and 1996, he appeared in episodes of ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' as different characters. In 1994, he appeared in the feature film ''[[Star Trek Generations]]''. In 2005, Thompson was cast as Admiral Valdore in three episodes of ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]''. Thompson has since participated in [[Trekkie|Star Trek fandom]], giving narrative [[DVD]] extras and appearing at conventions.{{cite web|last1=Anderson|first1=Phillip|title=Interviews: Brian Thompson - actor, "X-Files"/"Star Trek"/"Key West"/"Dragonheart"|url=http://www.kaos2000.net/interviews/brianthompson/|website=KAOS 2000|access-date=October 28, 2014|location=San Diego Comic Con International|date=July 22, 2000|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170927093302/http://www.kaos2000.net/interviews/brianthompson/|archive-date=September 27, 2017|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|last1=T'Bonz|title=APRIL-MAY 2014 TREK CONVENTIONS AND APPEARANCES|url=http://www.trektoday.com/content/2014/03/april-may-2014-trek-conventions-and-appearances/|website=Trek Today|access-date=October 28, 2014|date=March 31, 2014}} ==Personal life== Thompson is a [[standup paddleboarding]], [[windsurfing]], and [[kiteboarding]] enthusiast, and also studies [[hapkido]].{{cite news|last1=Wedlan|first1=Candace|title=Hapkido Helps Put the Wind in His Sails|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1998-apr-13-he-38745-story.html|access-date=October 28, 2014|work=Los Angeles Times}} He has two children. ==Selected filmography== ===Film=== {| class="wikitable sortable" |- ! '''James Joseph Sloyan Jr.'''<ref name="aos obit" /><ref name="jjs obit" /> (February 24, 1941 – July 22, 2026) was an American character actor of stage and screen, as well as a much-employed voice actor, most notably via his two-decade tenure as the voice of [[Lexus]]. He is the father of [[Samantha Sloyan]].

==Early life and career==
Sloyan was born in [[Indianapolis]], Indiana, on February 24, 1941.<ref name="Legacy">{{cite web |title=James SLOYAN|website=legacy.com |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/latimes/name/james-sloyan-obituary?id=62497894 |date=September 20, 2026}}</ref> One of four children, two girls and two boys, born to James J. Sloyan and Annamae O'Brien<ref name="aos obit">[https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-star/193126257/ "Obituaries: Annamae Sloyan"]. ''The Indianapolis Star''. August 23 1985. p. 47. Retrieved March 12, 2026. "Services for Annamae O'Brien Sloyan, 82, Albany, N.Y., formerly of Indianapolis and mother of actor James Sloyan, will be l0 a.m. Saturday in Assumption-St. Paul Catholic Church, Mechanicville. N.Y. The widow of James J. Sloyan, she died Wednesday in Albany Medical Center. A native of Mechanicville, she had been an Indianapolis resident many years before moving to Albany 30 years ago. Her son, an Indianapolis native, has starred in several Broadway shows and two television series, including Oh Madeline with actress Madeline Kahn. [...] Survivors, besides her son. include a daughter. Judy Wilkes, and another son, Patrick J. Sloyan."</ref><ref name="jjs obit">[https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-star/193131953/ "SLOYAN]. ''The Indianapolis Star''. 1954. Sec. 3, p. 7. Retrieved March 12, 2026. "James J.. 3490 E. Fall Creek Pkwy., N. Dr.. husband of Annamae, father of Patrick J., James J. Jr., and Judy, also survived by 3 sisters. Anna Sloyan, Mrs. Josephine Grampp of New York. [...] [S]ervices and burial Monday at Mechanicsville, N.Y.."</ref> (another being [[Pulitzer Prize]]-winning journalist [[Patrick J. Sloyan]]<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-post-star/193130053/ "Obituaries: Ann Judith (Judy) Wilkes (Oct. 8, 1935—Jan. 11, 2022)"]. ''The Post-Star''. January 23, 2022. p. C6. Retrieved March 13, 2026. "Judy was born Oct. 8, 1935 to the late Annamae (O’Brien) and James Sloyan in Stamford, CT, and had three siblings: Pulitzer Prize winning journalist, Patrick Sloyan (d. 2019, m. Phyllis); Elizabeth Sloyan (d. 1949); stage/film/television actor, James Sloyan (m. Deirdre)."</ref>), Sloyan Jr. spent most of the next nine and a half years in Europe, namely Italy, Switzerland, Ireland, and—if only long enough to board the next ship bound for home—Paris, France,<ref>"New York, New York Passenger and Crew Lists, 1909, 1925-1958", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:24TG-L62 : Sun Apr 13 03:58:40 UTC 2025), Entry for James Sloyan, 1950.</ref> before dividing the remainder of his preteens/adolescence between three decidedly disparate New York State municipalities. 1) [[Mechanicville, New York|Mechanicville]], the birthplace of Sloyan's mother<ref name="aos obit"/>; 2) [[Albany, New York|Albany]], the state capitol, where, by his own count, Sloyan was "actually thrown out of five [or] six high schools"<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/article/st-louis-post-dispatch/193118358/ "Network Bio"]. ''St. Louis Post-Dispatch''. April 10, 1977. p. 56.</ref>, and  3) New York City, where in 1957, Sloyan embarked on his scholarship-subsidized two years of study at the [[American Academy of Dramatic Arts]].<ref name="STFAQ20"/> 

Sloyan's acting career was interrupted in 1962, when he was drafted into the [[United States Army]] during the [[Vietnam War]].<ref name="STFAQ20">Clark, Mark (2013). ''[https://www.google.com/books/edition/Star_Trek_FAQ_2_0_Unofficial_and_Unautho/dWBfAgAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=1940+February+24+%22James+sloyan%22&pg=PT198&printsec=frontcover Star Trek: FAQ 2.0: EVERYTHING LEFT TO KNOW ABOUT THE NEXT GENERATION, THE MOVIES AND BEYOND (UNOFFICIAL AND UNAUTHORIZED)]''. Milwaukee, WI: Applause Theatre & Cinema Books. {{ISBN|978-1-55783-793-6}}.</ref>

==Television==
Sloyan's television career includes numerous brief performances on daytime dramas ''[[The Young and the Restless]], [[General Hospital]]'', and ''[[Ryan's Hope]]'', and guest appearances on prime-time series ''[[Hawaii Five-O (1968 TV series)|Hawaii Five-O]]''; ''[[The Streets of San Francisco]]''; ''[[Wonder Woman (TV series)|Wonder Woman]]''; ''[[Baywatch]]''; ''[[Moonlighting (TV series)|Moonlighting]]''; ''[[Quantum Leap (1989 TV series)|Quantum Leap]]''; ''[[The X-Files]]''; ''[[MacGyver (1985 TV series)|MacGyver]]''; ''[[Party of Five]]''; ''[[Matlock (1986 TV series)|Matlock]]''; ''[[Murder, She Wrote]]''; and ''[[Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman]]''. He appeared in the [[Made-for-television|television movies]] ''[[Blind Ambition (miniseries)|Blind Ambition]]'', ''[[Billionaire Boys Club (1987 film)|Billionaire Boys Club]]'', and ''My Son Is Innocent''.

In the fall of 1970, Sloyan, [[James Broderick]], and [[Reni Santoni]] were cast in the ''[[ABC Movie of the Week]]'' episode, "[[Panic on the 5:22]]", as a trio of underprivileged, disaffected, and somewhat desperate [[Bronx]] residents who board a suburbs-bound commuter train in [[Manhattan]] and, after donning ski masks and drawing guns, commandeer its [[parlor car|club car]] in hopes of making a quick killing.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/article/cumberland-evening-times/193803212/ "Hoods Menace Passengers"]. ''Cumberland Times-News''. Nov 9, 1974. p. 12. Retrieved March 20, 2026. "Three gunmen looking quick "score," hold-up affluent passengers aboard the club car of a swank New commuter train in "Panic The 5:22,' [...] Harvey Hart directed the Eugene Price screenplay that pits the trio of bumbling but dangerous hoodlums, frustrated graduates of a teenage gang in the Bronx, against a problem-ridden group of Manhattan business executives, a promiscuous high fashion New York model, a retired Army general, a brittle female cosmetic firm owner, a young attorney and a professional athlete."</ref><ref name="cameron">{{Cite news|title=Television Review: Panic on the 3:22|author=Cameron, Sue|date=November 21, 1974|work=The Hollywood Review|page=6|quote='Panic on the 5:22' is a 'disaster film' with a message. Instead of being held prisoner in a burning building or running from an earthquake, a group of wealthy people are held hostage and robbed at gunpoint in the club car of a commuter train. The three criminals represent the underprivileged slum people and the passengers represent everything the robbers want most and hate at the same time. In other words, it's a class confrontation on a train, with the robbery used as a tool for the message. It's a better-than-average MOW that just moves right along suspensefully. James Sloyan, Robert Walden and Reni Santoni give excellent performances as the crooks. [...] Quinn Martin was executive producer and Anthony Spinner produced. It was written by Eugene Price and directed by Harvey Hart.|id={{ProQuest|2931983431}}}}</ref><ref name="thomas">Thomas, Kevin (November 20, 1974). [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times/193304619/ "A Morality Play in 'Panic'"]. ''[[The Los Angeles Times]]''. pt. IV, p. 20. Retrieved March 20, 2026. "Robert Walden and his pals from long-ago teenage gang days, dim-witted Reni Santoni and nervous James Sloyan, board a train at Grand Central Station bound for Groton, Conn., [...] In the 35 minutes--minus commercials - before Walden and company don ski masks and draw their guns, Hart and Price show their wealthy would-be victims as largely unsympathetic types, for the most part arrogant, self-centered and, in a few instances, downright crooked. Thus, the difference between these rich passengers and the intruders is one of socio-economics rather than morals."</ref> Much to their dismay, these hopes are promptly dashed, and their desperation dramatically escalated, by the discovery that these affluent suburbanites carry nothing but credit cards.<ref>Halliwell, Leslie (1977). ''[https://archive.org/details/halliwellsfilmgu0000hall_e0p8/page/574/mode/2up?q=%22panic+on+the%22+%22w+eugene+price+d+harvey+hart%22 Halliwell's Film Guide : A Survey of 8,000 English-Language Movies]''. London: Granada Publishing. p. 574–575. {{ISBN|0246109823}}. "Wealthy passengers are terrorized by three incompetent hoodlums who are exasperated at finding credit cards instead of money. Smooth, odd little suspenser which goes on too long and submerges in cliche philosophy. Some smart moments, though."</ref> In 1972, Sloyan co-starred with [[James Coco]] in [[Neil Simon]]'s "The Greasy Spoon", one of five sketches that comprise his dark comedy, ''The Trouble With People'', presented by ''Bell System Television Theatre'' on [[NBC-TV]].<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-ouachita-citizen/193145336/ "Hooked by a Crook?"]. ''The Ouachita Citizen''. November 2, 1972. p. 7-B. Retrieved March 12, 2026. "'The Greasy Diner' has more than grease in store for James Coco as he finds out. Coco and Jim Sloyan star in 'The Greasy Diner,' one of the five sketches in the NBC-TV. Bell System Family Theatre presentation of Nell Simon's 'The Trouble With People,' which will be presented Sunday, Nov. 12, from 8-9 p.m."</ref> 

He appeared in a number of science fiction television series, including ''[[Buck Rogers in the 25th Century (TV series)|Buck Rogers in the 25th Century]]'', in which he portrayed Barnard "Barney" Smith in the episode "The Plot to Kill a City", and several roles in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise. In ''[[Star Trek: The Next Generation]]'', he portrayed Alidar Jarok (a defecting Romulan admiral) in "[[The Defector (TNG episode)|The Defector]]", and [[Alexander Rozhenko]] (Worf's son) as an adult in the future, in "[[Firstborn (Star Trek: The Next Generation)|Firstborn]]" using the alias "K'mtar". In ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'', he portrayed the Bajoran scientist [[List of recurring characters in Star Trek: Deep Space Nine#Doctor Mora Pol|Doctor Mora Pol]], [[Odo (Star Trek)|Odo's]] guardian scientist in the episodes "[[The Begotten]]" and "[[The Alternate (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|The Alternate]]". The ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'' episode "[[Jetrel]]" features Sloyan as the title character. 
{{clear|left}}

==Film==
Sloyan is featured in ''[[The Sting]]'' as Mottola, who is used to illustrate the concept of a griftee, in a variation on the [[pigeon drop]] scam.

He played roles in ''[[The Traveling Executioner]]'' (1970),<ref>Hale, Ernest (September 27, 1970). [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-columbus-ledger/193134067/ "Flicker Footnotes: 'Executioner' Is Sardonic Tale"]. ''The Columbus Ledger''. p .18. Retrieved March 13, 2026. "James J. Sloyan (r) as Deputy Warden Piquant, talks with prisoners in 'The Traveling Executioner'."</ref> ''[[The Gang That Couldn't Shoot Straight]]'' (1971), and ''[[Xanadu (film)|Xanadu]]'' (1980).

==Advertisements==
For 20 years, Sloyan was the [[voice-over|voice]] of Lexus. The company's first commercial, "[[Balance (advertisement)|Balance]]," aired in 1989 and went on to win several awards as well as homages in pop culture and media. Sloyan served as Lexus' sole voice actor until 2009.<ref name="STFAQ20"/> He later narrated ads for Mitsubishi.{{fact|date=September 2015}}
Sloyan was also a voice actor for [[Sprint Nextel]] long-distance services, and in film trailers for movies such as ''[[Jumper (2008 film)|Jumper]]'', ''[[The Shadow (1994 film)|The Shadow]]'', and ''[[How to Make an American Quilt]]''.<ref>[http://www.cedvoices.com/search_results.php?pageoffset=420&keyword=&mode=region&FileNameID=&search=5&subcat= CED Voices.com<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Sloyan and actress [[Deirdre Lenihan]] began dating in 1963 and became engaged five years later.<ref name="Cincinnati1973">{{cite news |last=Hoffman |first=Steve |title="TV and Radio: Lenihan May Be a New TV Sensation"|work=The Cincinnati Enquirer |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-cincinnati-enquirer/193113384/ |date=June 27, 1973 |page=20}}</ref> By 1973, they were openly living together, and seemed poised to take the plunge.<ref name="Boston1973">{{cite news |last=Shain |first=Percy |title=Deirdre Lenihan Proves Enchanting Newcomer |work=Boston Sunday Globe |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe/193112784/ |date=November 25, 1973 |page=92}}</ref> They had two children, Daniel Sloyan and actress [[Samantha Sloyan]].<ref name="nse1977">{{cite news |last=Terry |first=Carol Burton |title=TV Line |work=Newsday (Suffolk Edition) |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/newsday-suffolk-edition/193184078/ |date=May 15, 1977 |page=337}}</ref><ref name="stpd1977">{{cite news |title=Sloyan Bio|work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/st-louis-post-dispatch/193119924/ |date=April 10, 1977 |page=194}}</ref>

Sloyan died at his home in [[Sherman Oaks, California]], on July 22, 2026, at the age of 85.<ref name="Legacy"/><ref name="THR">{{cite news |last1=Barnes |first1=Mike |title=James Sloyan, Actor in ‘The Sting,‘ ‘Xanadu’ and ‘Oh Madeline,’ Dies at 85 |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/james-sloyan-dead-the-sting-oh-madeline-xanadu-1236706919/ |access-date=21 September 2026 |publisher=The Hollywood Reporter |date=21 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=MSN |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/entertainment/general/star-trek-s-james-sloyan-dies-at-the-age-of-85/ar-AA2cHtYg?ocid=msedgntp&pc=NMTS&cvid=6ab1b35a8d374532b0ceaa967429163e&ei=10 |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=www.msn.com}}</ref>
